TAC-4124... rcf define freeze CLI verb interfaces1 deps0 draft

TAC-4124-define-freeze - rcf define freeze CLI verb

Purpose: src/cli/freeze.js is the only writer of rcf/define/freeze.json in the shipped product. It composes readiness (REQ-175) with the freeze-record writer (REQ-172): one call to computeReadiness, one conditional call to saveFreezeRecord, one section 2.5 summary line, one exit code. The verb is the visible contract slice 4's bundle --next and slice 5's viewer read against; no other verb writes the freeze record.

Responsibilities

  • src/cli/freeze.js: parseArgs contract with --ack (multiple), --reason (multiple), --note, --litmus-attested (comma-separated D-names), --status, --json, --help; exit codes 0 success / 2 usage / 4 refused-on-failing.
  • src/cli/freeze.js: --ack argument validation runs before any tree load and refuses unknown gates and mismatched --ack/--reason pair counts with exit 2 and a stderr message naming the accepted set (define.shapes | define.crosscut | define.consistency with their short-name aliases).
  • src/cli/freeze.js: build tree + freeze + ledgers + testPointers concurrently (Promise.all mirroring readiness), then runWithAdmissibilityGate around computeReadiness, then apply --ack acknowledgements into an in-memory freeze.gates map keyed by gate id and recompute state per WARN_WITH_ACK stage.
  • src/cli/freeze.js: on any remaining 'failing' stage after acks, print the failing-stage block on stderr and exit 4 without writing.
  • src/cli/freeze.js: on freezeable, assemble the record body: reuse delta.js currentHashes generator (recompute matching what computeDelta uses so treeHash and docHashes agree with computeReadiness's currentTreeHash), derive counts, write the record via saveFreezeRecord, and print the section 2.5 summary (or --json envelope).
  • src/cli/freeze.js: --status branch runs no gates and never writes; it loads the record and computeDelta (unfrozen path when record absent) and prints the summary block, or emits { record, delta } on --json.
  • src/define/freeze-record.js: validateFreezeRecord requires override as a nullable field (throws FreezeRecordError field 'override' when the key is missing); loadFreezeRecord defaults a missing key to null so older records load; saveFreezeRecord's own validate step catches a caller that forgets to write override.
  • src/cli/readiness.js and CHANGELOG.md: replace ' -- ' with a colon in the two spots the brief calls out.
  • bin/rcf.js and src/cli/help.js: register the freeze verb (GROUPS.define.freeze, HELP_MAP.define.freeze, DEFINE_HELP listing).
  • Version reading: rcfLite from packages/rcf-lite/package.json (read once, cached via ESM import), ruleset from src/ruleset/ruleset.json's rulesetVersion or the umbrella version depending on the ruleset shape, schemas from node_modules/@stravica-ai/rcf-schemas/package.json (fall back to the manifest.schemasVersion when the package cannot be read).

Internal structure: One CLI module, three top-level branches by flag: --help early exit; --status branch (readRecord, computeDelta, format); default freeze branch (loadEverything, runReadiness, applyAcks, decideExit, writeRecord, formatSummary). Ack parsing is a small helper that walks the multi-valued --ack and --reason arrays in parallel, matching each ack gate to the next reason; a mismatch is a UsageError the caller catches. Counts derivation reuses tree.kindById to bucket ids into { req, us, ac, tac, adr, fbs }; the AC bucket walks every US and every US's acceptanceCriteria[]; acByClass parses the leading '[<class>]' marker using gates.js parseAcClass; interfaces bucketing walks every TAC's interfaces[] and buckets by kind. The 'first freeze' path is decided by (loadFreezeRecord() === null) BEFORE the freeze runs; branch is not re-derived from delta shape.

Interfaces

  • rcf define freeze (cliCommand) - The freeze CLI verb; the single interface this TAC ships.

Notes: Slice-4 hook (bundle --next): reads freeze.gates and freeze.frozenAt to decide the impacted-FBS printout; the impactedFbs field is not on the record yet (it is a computed shape). Slice-5 hook (viewer): renders the section-2.5 summary from the record + a fresh computeDelta call over the live tree. Litmus attestation seam (proposal section 9 decision 7): the --litmus-attested flag records the operator's per-decision attestation; the --litmus <n> real-dispatch runner is a named 0.30 seam (slice 6).

TAC-4127... Readiness viewer tab and shared pill, findings-list and diff components interfaces5 deps0 draft

TAC-4127-readiness-view - Readiness viewer tab and shared pill, findings-list and diff components

Purpose: Render the computeReadiness object as tab 1 of the HTML review surface so the viewer and `rcf define readiness --json` share one source of truth. Factor the three visual roles the tab needs (status pill, items list, before-after) into stable modules every tab can call. The tab is pure: it never recomputes readiness; the renderer takes the result object and the profile and emits one HTML string.

Responsibilities

  • src/view/readiness.js: renderReadinessPanel(result, { profile }) returns the eleven ordered blocks in spec section 5 as one HTML string: tree line (formatTreeLine), two verdict pills with formatVerdictLines strings as labels, two per-persona next-action lines, D1..D8 state chips with reason/acknowledgement text on hover, blockers grouped by persona (register orders the pair; non-register group collapses with count visible, never omitted), delta list grouped by REQ ancestor with document-level diff on changed items, per-stage check detail with persona pill and findings list when not ok, coverage tree-versus-delta with re-verify and re-execute counts, decisions outstanding in the #241 numbered format, a Freeze now control enabled iff levels.readyToBuild.ok, and the loaded freeze record.
  • src/view/readiness.js: deliberately imports nothing from src/query/ that is not already exported from src/query/index.js (formatVerdictLines, formatTreeLine, shortHash); the renderer never calls computeReadiness and never loads anything from disk.
  • src/view/components/pill.js: pill({ value, variant, title?, href? }) returns `<span class="rcf-pill rcf-pill--<variant> rcf-pill--<normalisedValue>" title?>{value}</span>` or an anchor when href is set; the normalisedValue is lowercased and `/` or spaces are collapsed to `-`.
  • src/view/components/findings-list.js: findingsList({ heading, count, items }) returns `<div class="rcf-findings-list"><h4>{heading} <span class="rcf-findings-list__count">{count}</span></h4><ul>...<li><a href={anchor}>{id}</a>: {why}</li>...</ul></div>` with ids capped at 20 and a `... N more suppressed` line beyond.
  • src/view/components/diff.js: diff(before, after) returns a two-column rendering of two document bodies for the delta list; criterion-level before-and-after is deferred per ADR-4127.
  • src/view/html-page.js: Readiness button and tabpanel are the first entries; the former Overview button and panel are relabelled PRD; the data-tab=overview and id=tab-overview identifiers are preserved so existing hash anchors still resolve; the inline-script TABS array gains 'readiness' as the first entry (default active tab) and keeps the existing four entries in order.
  • src/view/index.js: renderModelToPage loads the freeze record, ledgers, test pointers and profile text once, invokes computeReadiness via the pure src/query/ seam, and threads the result into the model so renderPage and renderContent carry one computed object; the SSE tree-update broadcast rewalks and recomputes on every change under rcf/.

Internal structure: readiness.js is a sequence of eleven small block builders calling the three shared components; each block consumes exactly one top-level field of the readiness result so a wire-level JSON diff ties to a visible block. The register ordering is picked once at the top via pickRegister (same helper the CLI uses) and threaded down. Hash anchors are built with the same `#<docId>` convention the existing tabs use so blocker-id links open the right tab and expand the right <details> through the existing resolveHash routine.

Interfaces

  • renderReadinessPanel (other) - [draft] Build the Readiness tab inner HTML from the readiness result and the operator profile; pure, no I/O, no recompute.
  • pill (other) - [draft] Render one rcf-pill span (or anchor) with a vocabulary class per value.
  • findingsList (other) - [draft] Render a heading plus id-anchor list with per-id why strings; ids capped at 20.
  • diff (other) - [draft] Render two document bodies side by side; document-level only in 0.29.0.
  • pickRegister (other) - [draft] Decide persona ordering from profile.md text; same contract as the CLI helper (productOwner | engineer | unstated).

Notes: The 0.29.0 scope keeps the diff component document-level only; criterion-level before-and-after is deferred to the UX review per ADR-4127. The pill component is additive and never changes the Product Map `pm-mini` or Requirements `status-chip` markup in this PR; those swaps are follow-ups once a mechanical mapping is established.

TAC-4128... DEFINE-stage guidance, prompts and managed rules interfaces3 deps0 draft

TAC-4128-define-guidance - DEFINE-stage guidance, prompts and managed rules

Purpose: serve the DEFINE-stage guidance pages, the argument-free MCP prompts and the managed-block rules that steer the harness through intake and the question loop.

Responsibilities

  • guidance/define-intent.md: the PO-register loop content from spec section 1.1, 1.2 and 1.4 as operator prose; wording rules for the PO register; what to print at the end.
  • guidance/elicitation-playbook.md: the L-sized restructure named in spec section 6 (sections 2 to 8 around D1 to D8 over the delta, the PO loop as the first worked example and the CSV feature as the second).
  • guidance/managed/agent-instructions-block.md: the two rules of spec section 6 last row - the PO-session rule and the prototype rule. The managed block regeneration never removes an existing rule.
  • guidance/manifest.json: register the new slug `define-intent`, the `rcf://docs/define-intent` resource, and the two new argument-free prompts `rcf_define_intent` and `rcf_define_intake`.
  • serves `rcf_define_intent` and `rcf_define_intake` prompts and the two managed-block rules of REQ-186 and REQ-187.

Internal structure: The MCP prompt and resource plumbing (src/mcp/prompts.js, src/mcp/resources.js) already serves manifest-registered entries byte-faithfully; this TAC only adds entries and markdown files. The managed block is regenerated by `rcf doctor` from the fragment in guidance/harness-template.md; the two new rules append to that fragment, and the regeneration pass preserves rules the project authored outside the managed markers.

Interfaces

  • rcf_define_intent (other) - Argument-free MCP prompt served from guidance/define-intent.md.
  • rcf_define_intake (other) - Argument-free MCP prompt served from the intake prompt markdown.
  • rcf://docs/define-intent (other) - Resource URI backed by guidance/define-intent.md.

Notes: This TAC was authored by PR 2 after the guidance slice did not land on origin/main under its reserved id ADR-4128 / TAC-4128; the shift is recorded in the PR 2 report. Later DEFINE PRs may expand it with further prompts and managed rules.

TAC-4129... the questions compute and the questions verb interfaces5 deps0 draft

TAC-4129-define-questions - the questions compute and the questions verb

Purpose: compute and print the persona question set.

Responsibilities

  • src/query/questions.js exposes computeQuestions(readiness, { tree, ledgers, profileText, persona }). It reads levels.intentComplete.blockedBy for persona productOwner or personas.engineer.blockers for persona engineer, expands each blocker's failing items into one question each via a per-check template, orders them D1 then D2 then D4 then D7 then by source span, carries one writeBack entry per `when` case the template defines, groups by source span, and never creates or modifies a file under rcf/.
  • src/cli/questions.js registers `rcf define questions [--json] [--persona productOwner|engineer] [--stage <D|short>] [--limit <n>]`. Persona default comes from the profile register, else productOwner. Text mode prints groups and asks; --json emits the computeQuestions object. Exit 0 always; unknown persona exits 2 with usage naming productOwner and engineer. Writes nothing under rcf/.
  • src/mcp/tools.js adds `rcf_define_questions` (same object as the verb's --json), `rcf_define_readiness` (the readiness object), and `rcf_define_ledger` (thin wrapper over the ledger handler). All three share the envelope the existing query and write tools use.

Internal structure: computeQuestions is a pure function: it folds the readiness blockers into questions through a per-check template table, deterministically ids each question from (stage, check, itemId), carries writeBack commands verbatim, and groups by source span (the trailing `(source: path:line-span)` marker on brief statements, else `tree`). The CLI verb runs the same walkTree + loadAllLedgers + loadFreezeRecord + readProfileText path readiness.js uses, calls computeReadiness, then computeQuestions. The MCP tools reuse the handler shape of the existing query tools (walkTree, okResult, usageErrorResult).

Interfaces

  • computeQuestions (moduleApi) - Compute the persona question set from a readiness result, a tree, the four ledgers and the profile text. Returns an object with treeHash, persona, level, ok, remaining, groups[], questions[], optional[] and engineer (collapsed count on the PO return).
  • rcf define questions (cliCommand) - Print or JSON-emit the persona question set. --persona defaults to the profile register. --stage narrows to one stage; --limit caps the questions array. Writes nothing under rcf/.
  • rcf_define_questions (other) - MCP tool: same structuredContent as the verb's --json output.
  • rcf_define_readiness (other) - MCP tool: the readiness object.
  • rcf_define_ledger (other) - MCP tool: thin wrapper over the ledger handler, taking { name, verb, ...flags }.

Notes: The viewer owns the Readiness tab PO-facing surface (viewer refresh PR 8); this TAC supplies only the data shape and the verb. Prompts and guidance land under TAC-4128.

TAC-4130... document intake into the brief ledger interfaces3 deps0 draft

TAC-4130-define-intake-brief - document intake into the brief ledger

Purpose: marker parser, scan wiring, `--findings` to open-question statements for `brief add --from`.

Responsibilities

  • src/define/ledgers.js parseBriefFromFile parses a leading `[kind]` marker and a trailing `(source: ...)` marker on each non-empty line; a line without `[kind]` takes `--kind` (default `capability`); a line without `(source: ...)` takes `--source` or the file path; `?`-, `TBC`-, `TBD`-, `Open:`- and `Question:`-leading lines kind `openQuestion` unless a marker says otherwise; an unknown `[kind]` raises LedgerError code 'usage' before any write; a 0.29.0 line-per-statement file parses unchanged.
  • src/cli/ledger.js `brief add` wires `--scan` / `--no-scan` (default on with `--from`, off with `--text`); runs the mechanical scans in src/intake/orchestrator.js over new statements against existing ones; `--findings <path>` accepts the shape `rcf discover intake --input` takes and makes one `openQuestion` statement per finding with `source: scan:<name>:<ids>`; `--dry-run` prints added + findings and writes nothing; `--json` emits `{ added: [...], findings: [...] }`; `--no-scan` together with `--findings` exits 2.
  • On a frozen tree the comparison set is every existing statement. Two statement files added in sequence scan the second against the first and the finding's `scan:` source names ids from both.

Internal structure: parseBriefFromFile returns drafts { text, kind, source } one per non-empty line. The CLI mints statements through addEntry; when scans are on it calls runIntakeScansOnDelta(newStatements, existingStatements) over the just-minted ids and the pre-existing body, then appends one openQuestion per finding whose source names the scan and the involved ids. `--findings` reads a JSON object with a `validationFindings[]` array (the same shape `rcf discover intake --input` accepts) and converts each entry to an openQuestion statement whose text is `detail` and whose source is `scan:<kind>`. `--dry-run` composes the full plan with every finding already converted and writes nothing.

Interfaces

  • parseStatementFile (other) - [draft] Parse a statement file into drafts { text, kind, source } one per non-empty line, honouring the leading [kind] and trailing (source: ...) markers and the kind defaults the caller supplies.
  • runIntakeScansOnDelta (other) - [draft] Run the mechanical intake scans over the newly minted statements against every existing statement and return a flat findings array.
  • rcf define ledger brief add --from --scan --no-scan --findings --dry-run --json (cliCommand) - Add brief statements from a statement file, optionally running the intake scans and converting operator-supplied findings into openQuestion statements.

Notes: This TAC covers the writer-side intake wiring only. The question-computation surface and the Register-prompt replacement land in PR 2 and are not covered here.

TAC-4131... Build/DAG sub-tab: DagToolbar, DagCanvas, DagInspector and the unconnected lane interfaces3 deps0 draft

TAC-4131-build-dag-view - Build/DAG sub-tab: DagToolbar, DagCanvas, DagInspector and the unconnected lane

Purpose: Render the Build tab's DAG sub-tab as the dependency-depth layout the design doc section 7 names: a toolbar with Status / Area / Buildable-now / Critical-path / Show-unconnected filters, a scrollable canvas with HTML nodes and inline SVG edges laid by `dependsOnFbsIds` depth and `buildOrder` rows, an inspector with needs and waits-on links, and a toggled unconnected lane. The renderer is pure: it takes the built tree model, emits one HTML string, mounts no inline script and reads from no provider other than the model.

Responsibilities

  • src/view/doc-renderers/build.js (or an adjacent src/view/build-dag.js shared from it): renderBuildDag(model, { buildableIds, cycleIds }) returns the full DAG sub-panel HTML string - toolbar + grid + inspector shell + hidden unconnected lane - with every FBS node carrying `data-fbs-id`, `data-status`, `data-domain`, `data-depth`, `data-buildable`, `data-critical`, `data-unconnected` so the client wiring can filter and highlight without re-rendering.
  • Layout: columns are 0..maxDepth; depth is the longest chain length from `dependsOnFbsIds` to the root (0 for no dependency). Rows inside a column are `buildOrder` ascending with `fbsId` lexicographic tie-break. Nodes are fixed-width buttons; edges are cubic SVG paths with arrowheads from dependency to dependant. Cycle members are excluded from the depth layout and surfaced as a finding; non-cycle FBS still render.
  • Unconnected lane: FBS with no incoming and no outgoing dependency. Hidden by default; the toggle's count equals that set's size.
  • Critical path: longest chain by node count across the DAG (because `estimatedHours` is sparse per the gap in design doc section 7); members get `data-critical=1`.
  • src/view/page-init.js: wireBuildDag() mounts click-to-highlight (upstream outlines link, downstream outlines warning, rest dim), writes `#tab=build&sub=dag&entity=<id>` through the existing writeHash on select, reads `entity=` on load to restore the selection and auto-opens the unconnected lane when the selected id is unconnected; filter toggles mirror the toolbar state onto node data attrs and keep the current selection.
  • html-page.js: renderBuildPanel swaps the PR 5 placeholder for `renderBuildDag(model, ...)`; the Build/Specs sub-tab is unchanged, the SubTabStrip wiring from PR 5 is unchanged, the Build tab's BuildStats and page head stay in place.
  • style.css: adds `.rcf-dag-*` tokens (toolbar, grid, canvas, node, edge, inspector, unconnected lane) sized against the shared Stravica tokens so both light and dark themes work; the canvas owns its own vertical and horizontal overflow so the viewer never scrolls horizontally.

Internal structure: Three composition seams. (1) a pure graph helper (buildDagLayout(fbsItems)) returns `{ nodes: [{ id, title, status, domain, depth, buildOrder, acCount, size, buildable, direct: { needs, waits }, closure: { upstream, downstream }, critical, unconnected }], edges: [{ from, to }], cycles: string[], unconnectedIds: string[], criticalPathIds: string[], maxDepth }`; (2) renderDagToolbar / renderDagCanvas / renderDagInspector compose one HTML string from the layout; (3) page-init.js's wireBuildDag reads from the DOM only (data attrs on nodes, aria-pressed on toggles) and never recomputes the layout. Needs and waits-on in the inspector resolve from the same closure sets the layout carries, so the two surfaces cannot disagree.

Interfaces

  • renderBuildDag (other) - [draft] Build the Build/DAG sub-tab HTML - toolbar, canvas, inspector shell, unconnected lane - from the built tree model and the pre-computed buildable set.
  • buildDagLayout (other) - [draft] Pure projection of `fbsItems[].dependsOnFbsIds` into DAG nodes, edges, depth columns, closures, critical path and unconnected ids; cycles surface as a `cycles` list and their members are excluded from the depth layout.
  • wireBuildDag (other) - [draft] Client-side wiring for the DAG canvas: click-to-highlight, filters, `#tab=build&sub=dag&entity=` round-trip, hash-driven selection restore, Open-in-Specs navigation. Reads from the DOM; sends no outbound postMessage.

Notes: The v1 rcf-tools DAG is the reference: keep its tiers, click-to-highlight, filters and stats; fix its dark-only palette, missing inspector, orphan pile-up, missing deep links and two-direction scrolling. No new TS, FBS or CN entry is minted - viewer-code PRs do not grow the build-step graph. The pill component (REQ-181) renders every status pill in the inspector; the shared `findings-list` module reports the cycle finding so the toolbar carries the same vocabulary as the rest of the tabs.

Architectural decisions

55 of 55 visible
ADR-001 Local filesystem is the single source of truth accepted

ADR-001 - Local filesystem is the single source of truth

Status: accepted

Context: RCF Lite must guarantee that a project's RCF documents live in the source repository, beside the code. v1 tooling operated over the GitHub API rather than the local repo, which broke the in-repository differentiator and tied the tool to a network surface.

Decision: Every read and write targets the local rcf tree directly. No external service, cache or database mirrors the documents. The CLI, the MCP server and the build loop all reach the filesystem only through the document store.

Consequences: The tool works offline and stays harness-agnostic. There is no sync problem and no second source to drift. The cost is that any multi-user or hosted scenario is out of scope by construction, which matches the product boundaries.

Alternatives considered

  • GitHub API as source of truth - Read and write documents through the GitHub contents API as v1 did.
    Not chosen because: Breaks the in-repository differentiator, requires network access and hit the API single-file fetch limit on large documents.
  • Local database index - Keep the files but maintain a database index for fast queries.
    Not chosen because: Introduces a second source of truth that can drift; query volumes for a single project do not justify it.

ADR-002 Validate against the published schema bundle at boundaries accepted

ADR-002 - Validate against the published schema bundle at boundaries

Status: accepted

Context: A non-coder cannot catch a malformed RCF document by eye, and an AI agent left unchecked can drift the document shape silently. Validation has to be a property of the tool, not a discipline of the user.

Decision: Register the published @stravica/rcf-schemas bundle once at start-up and validate every document on load and before persist. Refuse to write any document that does not validate.

Consequences: On-disk state is always valid. A small validation cost runs on every operation. The published schema package is the single source of truth for shape; local drift is impossible.

Alternatives considered

  • Local copies of the schemas - Vendor the schemas into the tool repository and validate against the local copy.
    Not chosen because: Allows local copies to drift from the published contract; the whole point of publishing the schemas is that every consumer keys to the same version.
  • Validate only on persist - Skip validation on load to save the cost of validating documents already on disk.
    Not chosen because: Misses drift caused by edits made outside the tool; load validation is what makes broken trees visible to the owner.

ADR-003 Plain JavaScript, no TypeScript pin accepted

ADR-003 - Plain JavaScript, no TypeScript pin

Status: accepted

Context: v1 was TypeScript-heavy and the build pipeline was a maintenance burden out of proportion to the project size. The product is small enough that boundary validation can carry the safety types would, and contributors should not have to set up a TypeScript toolchain to read or edit the code.

Decision: Build Lite is Node 24 ESM, plain JavaScript with JSDoc where types help. Schema validation at boundaries does the work compile-time types would otherwise do.

Consequences: Lower friction for contributors and a faster iteration loop. Some IDE assistance is given up. The team accepts that giving up in exchange for the simpler stack.

Alternatives considered

  • TypeScript everywhere - Author the tool in TypeScript with a tsc build step.
    Not chosen because: Adds a toolchain dependency for a small project; boundary validation carries the safety guarantee instead.
  • JSDoc plus checkJs - Use JSDoc with TypeScript checkJs to get partial type checking without authoring TypeScript.
    Not chosen because: Worth considering later if friction grows; not the round-1 default because the schema bundle is already the load-bearing contract.

ADR-004 Thin adapters over a shared core accepted

ADR-004 - Thin adapters over a shared core

Status: accepted

Context: The same operations are reached from the CLI, the MCP server and the build loop. Putting behaviour in any surface guarantees drift between surfaces.

Decision: Put every behaviour in a shared core module set. The CLI, the MCP server and the build loop are thin adapters that map their surface verbs to core operations and render results. The core's internal API is the stable contract.

Consequences: One behaviour, many surfaces, no drift between how a verb behaves on the CLI versus over MCP. The adapters carry no business logic so they are small and easy to keep in step.

Alternatives considered

  • Per-surface implementations - Implement each verb separately for the CLI and for MCP.
    Not chosen because: Guaranteed drift over time; the cost of duplication is paid forever in tests and bug reports.

ADR-005 MCP is local stdio only accepted

ADR-005 - MCP is local stdio only

Status: accepted

Context: Remote MCP cannot see the user's local codebase or RCF documents, which breaks the in-repository differentiator and the source-of-truth rule. The product is local-first by design; the MCP surface must follow.

Decision: The MCP server uses local stdio transport only. No network listener is opened. Remote MCP is excluded.

Consequences: The harness gets the full feature set with filesystem access. There is no hosted MCP path. The trade matches the local-filesystem source-of-truth rule and keeps the product boundaries clean.

Alternatives considered

  • Hosted MCP server - Run an MCP server over network transport with the user pointing it at a remote project.
    Not chosen because: Breaks the in-repository differentiator and the source-of-truth rule; a hosted surface would have to mirror or re-fetch the local tree.

ADR-006 Local-first preview is the default build outcome accepted

ADR-006 - Local-first preview is the default build outcome

Status: accepted

Context: The tool's target user is a non-coding owner who cannot self-verify a deployed application. Across the persona programme the one thing every such user could always exercise was the app running locally; a deployment could dead-end (run 03), be accepted-not-deployed (run 04), or pass locally yet fail in production (run 05). A build whose only demonstrable outcome lives on a remote runtime the owner cannot inspect leaves them with nothing they can check.

Decision: Every build lands, as its default outcome, a working and documented local preview loop - a dev server, seeded data where the app needs it, ideally reachable in one command. This holds whether or not the owner has stated a hosting target and whether they asked for a recommendation or not; local-first is the rock-solid default, and remote deployment is an addition on top of it, never a replacement for it. The elicitation and build-cycle guidance both carry this as a required deliverable, and the definition of done for a build includes the preview loop being present and documented.

Consequences: The owner always has a runtime they can drive and review, independent of any cloud account or deploy step. Local preview also becomes the honest substrate for the runtime-provenance discipline (ADR-008): a claim verified against local preview can say so truthfully. The cost is that a working local preview does not prove the deployed runtime works - which is precisely why provenance labelling and the interim self-review exist alongside this decision, not instead of it.

Alternatives considered

  • Deploy-first, preview optional - Treat a successful cloud deployment as the primary outcome and local preview as a nicety.
    Not chosen because: Strands owners whose deploy dead-ends or who decline to deploy, and hides defects behind a runtime they cannot inspect.
  • Preview only when the owner asks - Produce a local preview loop only when the owner explicitly requests one.
    Not chosen because: The owners who most need it are the least likely to know to ask; a default that depends on the user knowing the right question fails the target user.

ADR-007 Deploy target is elicited early and constrains the stack accepted

ADR-007 - Deploy target is elicited early and constrains the stack

Status: accepted

Context: Elicitation ran to a full RCF tree without ever establishing where the application would run. In run 03 the agent silently committed an entire Node-plus-node:sqlite stack that the owner's Cloudflare-only holdings could not host, dead-ending at deploy with no flag; run 04 chose the same incompatible stack class but disclosed it, and the difference was traced to that persona's contract forcing hosting into the spec early. The stack is a load-bearing architecture decision being made for a user who cannot judge it, and making it before the deploy target is known is how the G9 silent-architecture failure happens.

Decision: Elicitation establishes the deploy target early - a first-class elicitation item asked before the stack is committed, not inferred late - and the stack choice is constrained by the answer. When the owner does not know where it will run, the agent runs a jargon-free hosting-choice walkthrough (ADR captured separately in the guidance) rather than choosing silently. The deploy target and the stack constraint it implies are captured as an ADR on the project's own tree so the decision is visible and revisable.

Consequences: The stack the tool builds can actually be hosted where the owner can host it, and the hosting decision is surfaced instead of buried. Elicitation gains an early question the lite method did not previously carry, and the harness fragment gains a rule that a stack must not be committed before the deploy target is established. The cost is a small increase in elicitation length up front, paid back many times over against a dead-end at deploy the owner cannot diagnose.

Alternatives considered

  • Infer hosting from the stack later - Let the agent pick a stack on technical merit and determine hosting afterwards.
    Not chosen because: Produced the run-03 dead-end: a stack chosen before hosting is a stack that may have no host, discovered only at deploy.
  • Always ask the owner to choose a host explicitly - Require the owner to name a hosting provider during elicitation.
    Not chosen because: The target user often does not know the options; a bare demand to choose freezes them. The guidance must walk an unsure owner through choosing, not just ask.

ADR-008 Verification claims carry runtime provenance accepted

ADR-008 - Verification claims carry runtime provenance

Status: accepted

Context: In run 05 the tool's self-verification claimed the work was 'verified against a live Worker', but its end-to-end tests actually ran against wrangler dev on localhost, which does not enforce the Cloudflare edge PBKDF2 iteration cap. The result was 89/89 green tests, a confident verification claim, and a CRITICAL signup/login 500 on the actually-deployed runtime. The failure was not laziness but provenance: a claim implied a runtime it had never touched. A non-coding owner cannot tell 'verified against the deployed runtime' from 'verified against a local emulator', so the claim itself must carry the distinction.

Decision: Every 'verified' or 'tested' claim the tool or its agent makes names the runtime it was checked against - for example 'verified against wrangler dev (localhost) - NOT the deployed Worker runtime'. No claim may state or imply deploy-runtime verification that did not happen. The build-cycle guidance requires the runtime label on verification claims in the Test and Finalise stages and in the PR body's verification section; a claim without a named runtime is treated as incomplete.

Consequences: The owner can see exactly what was and was not proven, and the gap between 'passes locally' and 'works deployed' stops being invisible. This makes local preview (ADR-006) an honest thing to cite rather than a false proxy for deployment, and it defines the seam the interim self-review and the future independent gate target. The cost is that verification claims become longer and, deliberately, less reassuring - which is the point: an unlabelled claim was falsely reassuring.

Alternatives considered

  • Require verification against the deployed runtime - Mandate that every verification run against the real deployed target, removing the provenance ambiguity by removing local verification.
    Not chosen because: Not always possible for the owner (no deploy yet, no account), and it belongs to the productised independent gate (rcf verify-lite); the base offering's job is to label provenance honestly, not to force a deployed run.
  • Trust green suites as verification - Treat a passing test suite as sufficient evidence of 'verified'.
    Not chosen because: Run 05 is the counter-example: 89/89 green with a critical production failure. A green suite is evidence about the runtime it ran on and nothing more.

ADR-009 Interim self-review is guidance, not the independent gate accepted

ADR-009 - Interim self-review is guidance, not the independent gate

Status: accepted

Context: The persona programme showed self-verification is only as truthful as the runtime it verifies against, and that a green suite plus a confident claim can still ship a user-facing defect (runs 03 and 05). The durable answer is a productised independent verification gate (rcf verify-lite), being scoped separately at HQ. But the base offering needs a stopgap now, and it must not pretend to be the independent gate: an in-loop self-review by the same agent is not an independent check and cannot be sold as one.

Decision: The guidance carries interim self-review guidance - documentation and prompt-level, not a new subsystem - for a carefully-scoped manual-review subagent dispatch: a periodic review every few FBS builds plus one at the end of the build. The reviewer runs fresh-context, drives the APP against the acceptance criteria rather than reading the code, and targets the defect classes green suites miss: session-class bugs, false-promise UI (stubs that imply real actions), runtime mismatch (localhost versus deployed), dead auth paths, and dead code. The guidance states plainly that this is an interim stopgap until rcf verify-lite exists and that it is not the independent verification gate.

Consequences: The base offering gains a review step that catches the defect classes the five-stage loop demonstrably missed, at documentation cost and with no new code surface to maintain. Because it is guidance, it can ship now and be retired or folded into rcf verify-lite later without a migration. The cost and the honesty boundary are the same point: a same-programme reviewer is better than nothing and weaker than an independent gate, and the guidance says so rather than overclaiming. Update 2026-07-28: rcf verify-lite has since shipped and rcf build finalise runs it as the independent gate, so the 'stopgap until the gate exists' framing recorded in the decision above is spent. The decision itself stands - the self-review is still guidance, still not a subsystem, still not the gate - but it is now positioned as the cheap in-loop check that runs between builds, subordinate to the finalise gate rather than a placeholder for it, and AC-805-4 and the guidance were reworded to match.

Alternatives considered

  • Wait for rcf verify-lite - Ship no review step until the productised independent gate exists.
    Not chosen because: Leaves the base offering shipping the exact defect classes the programme caught, for months, against users who cannot catch them themselves.
  • Build an independent-gate subsystem now - Solve the independent-verification problem inside rcf-lite immediately.
    Not chosen because: That is a separate product being scoped at HQ; duplicating it here pre-empts a repo reshape and over-builds the lite tier. The Tier-1 scope is guidance, not a gate.

ADR-010 Blueprint conflict-topic vocabulary is a free-label lookup key (camelCase canonical on shipped blueprints) accepted

ADR-010 - Blueprint conflict-topic vocabulary is a free-label lookup key (camelCase canonical on shipped blueprints)

Status: accepted

Context: Round-1 of Phase 3.5 (w-2026-08-19-008) gate-tightened the topic vocabulary at the supersede writer by requiring topics to be kebab slugs; the SHIPPED SPA and REST blueprints declare their scope:global ADR topics in camelCase (authModel, errorEnvelope, clientRouting, theming, clientState, apiVersioning, logging), so following the reshaped conflict message's option 3 exactly as printed exited 2 with 'not a valid kebab slug' on every shipped topic. The 0.4.5 manifest schema is silent on topic character class (minLength: 1) and the schema docs cite errorEnvelope as an example. Gate-tightening past the schema is a first-class defect on this estate.

Decision: The blueprint conflict-topic vocabulary is a FREE LABEL — a lookup key used by the conflict detector (exact-match between an incoming ADR's declared topic and each applied ADR's declared topic) and by the resolution record (verbatim on manifest.resolutions[].topic). No character-class constraint beyond the schema's own minLength: 1 plus a writer-edge whitespace-only refuse. The shipped blueprint packs are canonical: their topics MUST be camelCase kebab-free single-word or camelCase identifiers (authModel, errorEnvelope, clientRouting, ...); new shipped blueprints follow the same convention. When a topic string must be projected into an id grammar that does require a kebab slug (specifically the scaffolded project-ADR id tail, whose grammar is `^ADR-\d{3,}(-[a-z0-9]+(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*)?$`), the writer kebab-ifies at the projection edge (`authModel` -> `ADR-NNN-auth-model`) and never at the vocabulary edge.

Consequences: The reshaped conflict message's option 3 executes verbatim from the refused-add state against the shipped SPA + REST blueprints. Topic strings on manifest.resolutions[].topic remain byte-identical to the topic strings on the applied blueprint's ADR.contributions[].topic, so exact-match lookup is trivial to reason about. Kebab-ification is confined to the project-ADR id tail; the same topic string may appear verbatim in the manifest and kebab-cased inside an ADR id in the same tree without conflict. Blueprint authors who ship non-camelCase topics (kebab-case, snake_case) still validate against the schema; the exact-match detector still functions; only the ADR id tail projection changes.

Alternatives considered

  • Enforce kebab-slug topics at the writer edge - Reject any topic string that is not `[a-z][a-z0-9]*(?:-[a-z0-9]+)*` at supersede and add --resolve.
    Not chosen because: Gate-tightens past the manifest schema (which is minLength: 1 with no character constraint), incompatible with the shipped SPA + REST blueprints' camelCase topic vocabulary, and made option 3 unexecutable as printed against the shipped packs.
  • Retroactively kebab-case the shipped blueprint packs' topics - Change SPA + REST blueprints to declare kebab topics (auth-model, error-envelope, ...); consumers migrate.
    Not chosen because: The blueprint packs are canonical content the mechanism serves; the mechanism does not get to dictate the packs' vocabulary. camelCase is a legitimate identifier shape (the schema examples confirm it).
  • Normalise topics at the detector - Fold both sides to a canonical form (kebab or lowercased-strip-nonalnum) before comparing.
    Not chosen because: Introduces vocabulary drift (two different topic strings comparing equal) and makes the operator's mental model of what matches what harder, not easier. Exact-match on the free label is the least surprising rule.

ADR-2214... Admin-console reads zeroTrustGate at apply-time and switches sign-in surface (recommendedDefault true) accepted

ADR-2214-application-admin-console-consume-zero-trust-gate - Admin-console reads zeroTrustGate at apply-time and switches sign-in surface (recommendedDefault true)

Status: accepted

Context: application-admin-console v1.0.0 shipped with principalDirectory as the sole hard requirement; sign-in surface was local per whatever security-auth-* was applied. Round-6 T-4 introduces edge-cloudflare-access with the zeroTrustGate capability; a composed deployment needs the admin-console to flip its sign-in surface deterministically.

Decision: application-admin-console v1.1.0 reads appliedCapabilities via readAppliedCapabilities at apply-time. When zeroTrustGate is present the sign-in surface renders access-gated (no local form, principal reads from request.auth); when absent the surface falls back to whatever security-auth-* is applied. Q4 default (spec 5.4.1): zeroTrustGate is CONSUMED OPTIONALLY; principalDirectory remains the sole hard requirement (making Access-gate hard is a v2.0 change). Standards trace clause: Cloudflare round 6 spec section 5.4 (admin-console v1.1.0 delta). recommendedDefault: true.

Consequences: The v1.1.0 admin-console remains backward-compatible with every v1.0.0 deployment. An Access-gated deployment automatically stops rendering the local login form; the local-login surface still ships in v1.1.0 (fallback branch when zeroTrustGate absent).

ADR-3501... Edge authentication gate: Cloudflare Access Zero-Trust JWT-assertion gate (scope global, new topic edgeAuthenticationGate) accepted

ADR-3501-edge-cloudflare-access-jwt-gate - Edge authentication gate: Cloudflare Access Zero-Trust JWT-assertion gate (scope global, new topic edgeAuthenticationGate)

Status: accepted

Context: T-4 repo-chain ADR mirror for the shipped blueprints/edge-cloudflare-access/contributions/adrs/adr-3501-edge-cloudflare-access-jwt-gate.json contribution. The chain slice is the audit trail for the JWT-gate decision (scope global on new topic edgeAuthenticationGate). Cloudflare Access enforces the Zero-Trust policy at the CF edge and passes a signed JWT to the origin Worker in the Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion header per https://developers.cloudflare.com/cloudflare-one/policies/access/. Every applied Worker needs one project-wide answer to the edgeAuthenticationGate topic; a future non-Cloudflare adapter conflicts on the same topic by design.

Decision: The shipped v1.0.0 default is Cloudflare Access's Zero-Trust JWT-assertion gate. The JWT validator (TAC-3501) is the sole reader of the Cf-Access-Jwt-Assertion header and reduces the principal into request.auth. The edgeAuthenticationGate topic scope is global on this blueprint; the topic string is edgeAuthenticationGate (lower camel case). Standards trace clause: Cloudflare Access policy actions and rule selectors.

Consequences: The applying project inherits Cloudflare's documented Access policy model and the JWT rotation cadence published at https://<team>.cloudflareaccess.com/cdn-cgi/access/certs. Consumers deploying to a non-Cloudflare edge reach for a sibling adapter blueprint that lands as a v1.x minor on this shelf.

ADR-3503... Policy scope: application-level (recommended default) or per-path elicited accepted

ADR-3503-edge-cloudflare-access-policy-scope - Policy scope: application-level (recommended default) or per-path elicited

Status: accepted

Context: Cloudflare Access binds a policy at the application level (one policy protects every path) or per-path. Application-level scope is the most common shape.

Decision: Recommended default is application-level (recommendedDefault: true); the elicited alternative is per-path. Standards trace clause: Cloudflare Access policy actions and rule selectors.

Consequences: A fresh project applying the blueprint gets one application-level policy; an operator opting into per-path scope elicits a route table.

ADR-3504... Audit retention window (metadata-only fields) is delegated to the applied logging companion accepted

ADR-3504-edge-cloudflare-access-audit-retention - Audit retention window (metadata-only fields) is delegated to the applied logging companion

Status: accepted

Context: The validator emits one audit event per outcome with the metadata-only shape {email, outcome, timestamp, path}. Long-term retention is a compliance decision an applied logging companion already answers.

Decision: Retention is delegated to the applied logging companion (suggestedCompanions[0]). The blueprint declares no retention policy of its own. Standards trace clause: generic enterprise practice.

Consequences: A workspace without a logging companion loses the audit events after the Worker context tears down; the guide names the trade.

ADR-3601... Human verification gate: Cloudflare Turnstile siteverify (scope global, new topic humanVerificationGate) proposed

ADR-3601-edge-cloudflare-turnstile-verifier-contract - Human verification gate: Cloudflare Turnstile siteverify (scope global, new topic humanVerificationGate)

Status: proposed

Context: T-5 repo-chain ADR mirror for the shipped blueprints/edge-cloudflare-turnstile/contributions/adrs/adr-3601-edge-cloudflare-turnstile-verifier-contract.json contribution. Cloudflare Turnstile documents a client widget plus a server-side siteverify endpoint (https://challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/siteverify) as the wire-shape contract per https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/. Every applied Worker needs one project-wide answer to the humanVerificationGate topic; a future non-Cloudflare adapter (hCaptcha, reCAPTCHA) conflicts on the same topic by design.

Decision: The shipped v1.0.0 default is Cloudflare Turnstile with server-side siteverify. The verifier POSTs {secret, response} to https://challenges.cloudflare.com/turnstile/v0/siteverify; on success:true the handler proceeds, on success:false the handler rejects 400 with the error-codes value. The humanVerificationGate topic scope is global on this blueprint. Standards trace clause: Cloudflare Turnstile siteverify endpoint documented shape.

Consequences: The applying project inherits Cloudflare Turnstile documented widget-and-siteverify contract per https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/. A future hCaptcha or reCAPTCHA sibling contributes the same humanVerificationGate topic with a different answer, forcing a deliberate operator-resolved conflict at the project ADR level.

Status: proposed

Context: Cloudflare Turnstile documents three widget modes per https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/: managed (Cloudflare decides when to show a challenge), non-interactive (always shows a non-interactive challenge) and invisible (mounts an invisible widget). The choice is a per-surface operational profile.

Decision: Widget mode is elicited (elicited: true). Values: managed, non-interactive, invisible. recommendedDefault: managed. The applied-sidecar records the operator answer per applying surface. Standards trace clause: Cloudflare Turnstile documented widget modes.

Consequences: The elicitation forces an explicit answer on every apply. The pack fixture accepts mode=managed, non-interactive or invisible and pins the invisible-widget test sitekeys (1x0000000000000000000000BB, 2x0000000000000000000000BB) alongside the managed pass/fail sitekeys so every mode is exercised.

ADR-3603... Refuse-if-token-missing status is 400 with an error-code body (no sitekey leak); siteverify failure carries the documented error-codes value proposed

ADR-3603-edge-cloudflare-turnstile-refuse-shape - Refuse-if-token-missing status is 400 with an error-code body (no sitekey leak); siteverify failure carries the documented error-codes value

Status: proposed

Context: Cloudflare Turnstile siteverify returns success:false with error-codes on failure; documented codes at https://developers.cloudflare.com/turnstile/. The applying project needs a stable refusal shape that never leaks the sitekey or the secret.

Decision: Refuse-if-token-missing status is 400. Refusal body carries a stable error-code (turnstile.token-missing for the guard branch, or the Cloudflare error-codes first entry for the siteverify-failure branch). Refusal body never carries the sitekey, the secret or the response token value. Standards trace clause: Cloudflare Turnstile documented error codes.

Consequences: The 400 status is machine-observable at every applied surface; downstream observability records the outcome by error-code, not by sitekey. Event records ship sitekeyHash, outcome and timestamp only (event-secrecy probe asserts this).

ADR-3701... Edge throttle contract: Cloudflare WAF rate-limiting rules (scope global, new topic edgeThrottleContract) proposed

ADR-3701-edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting-throttle-contract - Edge throttle contract: Cloudflare WAF rate-limiting rules (scope global, new topic edgeThrottleContract)

Status: proposed

Context: T-6 repo-chain ADR mirror for the shipped blueprints/edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting/contributions/adrs/adr-3701-edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting-throttle-contract.json contribution. An applying Workers project needs a zone-level guard that refuses over-threshold bursts at the CF edge before they reach the origin. Cloudflare's WAF rate-limiting rules provide the native answer with a documented rule shape (id, expression, threshold, period, characteristics, action, duration) per https://developers.cloudflare.com/waf/rate-limiting-rules/. Every applied Worker needs one project-wide answer to the edgeThrottleContract topic; a future non-Cloudflare edge-throttle sibling would conflict on the same topic.

Decision: The shipped v1.0.0 default is Cloudflare WAF rate-limiting rules as the zone-level edge throttle. The rule shape matches the Cloudflare documented fields. The edgeThrottleContract topic scope is global on this blueprint. Standards trace clause: Cloudflare WAF rate-limiting rules documented shape.

Consequences: The applying project inherits Cloudflare's documented rule shape and platform-imposed limits. Rule state lives on the Cloudflare account, not in the git tree; the local manifest under cloudflare/rate-limits/ is the source of truth. Drift risk is addressed via ADR-3704 (cadence) and TAC-3703 (drift-audit runner).

ADR-3702... Layering with security-auth-magic-link: zone rule OVER the per-email application rule proposed

ADR-3702-edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting-layering - Layering with security-auth-magic-link: zone rule OVER the per-email application rule

Status: proposed

Context: T-6 repo-chain ADR mirror for the shipped blueprints/edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting/contributions/adrs/adr-3702-edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting-layering.json contribution. The security-auth-magic-link blueprint ships a per-email per-minute application-level rate limiter on the mint surface; edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting ships a zone-level IP-per-URL rate rule at the CF edge. Without an explicit layering ADR the operator can mistake the two rules for overlapping.

Decision: When both blueprints apply, the zone rule sits at the CF edge and refuses the (N+1)th request for the elicited duration before it reaches the origin; the magic-link per-email rate limiter continues at the mint-surface. The two rules operate on different characteristic sets (IP-per-URL vs per-email per-minute) and are additive. recommendedDefault: true. Standards trace clause: generic enterprise practice.

Consequences: The composition is documented in the guide with a copy-paste example. The applied recorder records both blueprints so the operator sees the two-rule shape at apply time; drift into overlap is caught in the drift-audit runner.

ADR-3703... Manifest at cloudflare/rate-limits/, one JSON file per rule; operator applies via wrangler or dashboard proposed

ADR-3703-edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting-manifest-shape - Manifest at cloudflare/rate-limits/, one JSON file per rule; operator applies via wrangler or dashboard

Status: proposed

Context: T-6 repo-chain ADR mirror for the shipped blueprints/edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting/contributions/adrs/adr-3703-edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting-manifest-shape.json contribution. The rule set could be committed as a wrangler-shape script, a bespoke apply tool, a single manifest file, or one file per rule. Single-file hides diff signal when one rule changes; committed script couples the source of truth to a specific tool.

Decision: The manifest lives at the elicited rate-limit-rules-dir (default cloudflare/rate-limits/), with one JSON file per rule. No committed script writes rules to the live zone; the operator applies through the documented wrangler or dashboard flow per REQ-101 and TAC-3702. recommendedDefault: true. Standards trace clause: generic enterprise practice.

Consequences: One-file-per-rule keeps each rule diff scoped. No committed apply script means the blueprint does not couple to a tool version and does not require an API token at build time. Operator applies at their chosen cadence; drift risk is addressed via ADR-3704 and TAC-3703.

ADR-3704... Drift-audit cadence: off, daily or hourly (elicited; recommendedDefault daily) proposed

Status: proposed

Context: T-6 repo-chain ADR mirror for the shipped blueprints/edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting/contributions/adrs/adr-3704-edge-cloudflare-rate-limiting-drift-audit-cadence.json contribution. Rate-limit rules live on the Cloudflare account, not in the git tree. Drift in either direction (dashboard change without manifest update, manifest edit without an apply) is only surfaced if the applying project runs the drift-audit runner at a cadence.

Decision: The drift-audit cadence is elicited (rate-limit-drift-audit-cadence) with three options: off (disables the runner), daily (24-hour cadence), hourly (60-minute cadence). recommendedDefault: daily. elicited: true. Standards trace clause: generic enterprise practice.

Consequences: daily is safe for typical operations; hourly is safe for high-cadence rule changes; off is safe only when the operator has an alternative drift-check discipline. The elicit prompts at apply time.

ADR-3801... Cloud host contract: Hetzner Cloud VM as the shipped cloudHost shape (scope global, new topic linuxCloudHostContract) proposed

ADR-3801-deploy-hetzner-server-cloud-host-contract - Cloud host contract: Hetzner Cloud VM as the shipped cloudHost shape (scope global, new topic linuxCloudHostContract)

Status: proposed

Context: T-1 repo-chain ADR mirror for the shipped blueprints/deploy-hetzner-server/contributions/adrs/adr-3801-deploy-hetzner-server-cloud-host-contract.json contribution. An applying project needs a first-class Linux VM contract that container-orchestration and edge-ingress consumers can compose on. The Hetzner Cloud API server resource plus cloud-init user-data provides the shipped v1.0.0 shape per https://docs.hetzner.cloud/. Every applied cloud-host needs one project-wide answer to the linuxCloudHostContract topic; a future non-Hetzner sibling (Vultr, DigitalOcean, Fly.io) would conflict on the same topic.

Decision: The shipped v1.0.0 default is a Hetzner Cloud server as the linuxCloudHostContract provider. The provisioner reads its shape from the applying manifest and creates a matching live server via the hcloud verbs (or the raw Hetzner Cloud API when provisioningTool=raw-api). The linuxCloudHostContract topic scope is global on this blueprint. recommendedDefault: true. Standards trace clause: Hetzner Cloud API server resource and cloud-init user-data contract per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Consequences: Consumer blueprints that run on a Linux host (containers, systemd services, tunnel connectors) compose on capabilities: [cloudHost]. Rebuild-from-manifest is always possible: the manifest is the source of truth, the live server is derivative. Drift from the shipped manifest to the live server is out of scope for v1.0.0; a later minor may add a drift-audit runner.

ADR-3802... Snapshot cadence: weekly default, daily and off alternatives, Hetzner-managed backups elicited (scope global, new topic snapshotAndBackupCadence) proposed

ADR-3802-deploy-hetzner-server-snapshot-cadence - Snapshot cadence: weekly default, daily and off alternatives, Hetzner-managed backups elicited (scope global, new topic snapshotAndBackupCadence)

Status: proposed

Context: T-1 repo-chain ADR mirror for the shipped blueprints/deploy-hetzner-server/contributions/adrs/adr-3802-deploy-hetzner-server-snapshot-cadence.json contribution. An applying project needs a discipline for how often the Hetzner Cloud server takes a snapshot and whether Hetzner-managed backups are enabled. Hetzner documents snapshots as manual-fire on-demand and Hetzner-managed backups as a paid subscription at 20 percent of monthly server price per https://docs.hetzner.com/cloud/servers/backups-snapshots/overview. Every cloud host needs one project-wide answer to the snapshotAndBackupCadence topic.

Decision: The shipped v1.0.0 default is weekly snapshot cadence with the snapshot fired by a scheduled runner in the applying project. Alternatives elicited: daily (higher recovery-point-objective, higher storage) and off (no automatic snapshot). Hetzner-managed backups are an elicited paid opt-in that costs 20 percent of monthly server price per the vendor docs; when opted-in, the scheduled snapshot runner still fires so the two mechanisms compose. The snapshotAndBackupCadence topic scope is global on this blueprint. recommendedDefault: true. Standards trace clause: Hetzner Cloud backups-and-snapshots documented pricing and mechanism per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Consequences: Weekly snapshot on a cx23 costs approximately EUR 0.005 per month in extra storage; daily is approximately EUR 0.035; Hetzner-managed backups add approximately EUR 0.80 per month per server at cx23. The scheduled snapshot runner emits hetznerSnapshotTaken with snapshot id and wall-clock time so the observability sink surfaces the cadence.

ADR-3803... Provisioning tool: hcloud CLI default, raw Hetzner Cloud API alternative, Terraform rejected proposed

ADR-3803-deploy-hetzner-server-provisioning-tool - Provisioning tool: hcloud CLI default, raw Hetzner Cloud API alternative, Terraform rejected

Status: proposed

Context: T-1 repo-chain ADR mirror for the shipped blueprints/deploy-hetzner-server/contributions/adrs/adr-3803-deploy-hetzner-server-provisioning-tool.json contribution. An applying project needs a documented answer to how the provisioner shells out to Hetzner Cloud. Options considered: hcloud CLI (small, self-documenting, JSON output), raw Hetzner Cloud REST API (no CLI dependency, useful when the target host cannot install a binary), Terraform (declarative, adds a second toolchain and a state file). Baz ruling 2026-09-07 09:50Z on decision 18: hcloud not Terraform.

Decision: The shipped v1.0.0 default is the hcloud CLI as the provisioning tool. Alternative elicited: raw-api (the provisioner fetches the Hetzner Cloud REST API directly). Terraform is a rejected alternative: adds a second toolchain and a state file, neither of which matches the shelf shape (see section 9 of hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md). elicited: true. recommendedDefault: hcloud. Standards trace clause: Hetzner Cloud CLI documented resource verbs per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Consequences: The applying project installs the hcloud binary on the operator laptop and any CI runner that provisions. The raw-api fork is behind the same provisioner facade so no consumer code diverges. The provisioner-facade sole-reader guarantee holds on both paths.

ADR-3804... Hardening baseline: SSH key-only, root disabled, UFW default-deny, DOCKER-USER chain, fail2ban, unattended-upgrades proposed

ADR-3804-deploy-hetzner-server-hardening-baseline - Hardening baseline: SSH key-only, root disabled, UFW default-deny, DOCKER-USER chain, fail2ban, unattended-upgrades

Status: proposed

Context: T-1 repo-chain ADR mirror for the shipped blueprints/deploy-hetzner-server/contributions/adrs/adr-3804-deploy-hetzner-server-hardening-baseline.json contribution. Every Hetzner server exposed to the public internet needs a minimum hardening set. Cloud-init landing the set at first boot is the operator-friendly shape (declarative, reproducible, in git). The Debian unattended-upgrades wiki documents the auto-update mechanism; the estate baseline at operator/knowledge/systems/environments/hetzner-cloud/overview.md Security posture baseline names the exact block set.

Decision: The shipped v1.0.0 hardening baseline is the six blocks: SSH key-only (PasswordAuthentication no), root disabled (PermitRootLogin no), UFW default-deny incoming with 22 and 80 and 443 permitted per the manifest firewall shape, DOCKER-USER iptables chain wired to drop non-conforming egress, fail2ban SSH jail, unattended-upgrades on for security updates. The render-lint probe asserts every block appears in the rendered cloud-init YAML; a mutation removes a block and the probe FAILS naming the missing line. recommendedDefault: true. Standards trace clause: Debian unattended-upgrades wiki AND the estate baseline at operator/knowledge/systems/environments/hetzner-cloud/overview.md Security posture baseline per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Consequences: The applying project inherits the six-block baseline on every provisioned server. Deviation costs a fresh ADR at the applying project level. The baseline is text plus a rendered template; extension (extra ssh key, extra fail2ban jail) sits on top without rewriting.

ADR-3901... T-2 container host contract: docker compose as source of truth (scope global, new topic containerHostContract) accepted

ADR-3901-platform-docker-compose-host-contract - T-2 container host contract: docker compose as source of truth (scope global, new topic containerHostContract)

Status: accepted

Context: An applying project running its stack on a Linux cloudHost needs one shipped contract for how services are declared, wired and brought up on a container-orchestration surface. Round-7 T-2 mints the containerHostContract topic on this ADR. Docker Compose is the shipped v1.0.0 surface (compose.yaml as source of truth, healthchecks required, secrets as files, restart discipline, reverse-proxy as artefact). Every applied container host needs one project-wide answer to the containerHostContract topic; a future non-compose sibling (Docker Swarm, Nomad) would contribute the same topic string with a different mechanism, forcing a DELIBERATE conflict the operator resolves per the round-2 conflict pattern. Standards trace clause: Docker Compose file reference AND Docker Engine install-on-Ubuntu docs per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Decision: The shipped v1.0.0 default is docker compose on a cloudHost as the containerHostContract provider. A canonical compose.yaml at the repo root drives docker compose up on the applied cloudHost (T-1 deploy-hetzner-server); healthchecks refuse at docker compose config on missing; secrets are file mounts; restart policies are unless-stopped or on-failure; the reverse-proxy config is a first-class versioned artefact per TAC-3904. The containerHostContract topic scope is global on this blueprint; the topic string is containerHostContract (lower camelCase, one concept per topic, no version suffix, per the round-2 rules-for-new-topics clause on the shelf registry). Standards trace clause: Docker Compose file reference AND Docker Engine install-on-Ubuntu docs per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Consequences: Consumer blueprints that ship as containers declare capabilities: [containerHost] on their applied contract; the round-7 T-3 edge-cloudflare-tunnel reads this capability at apply-time to choose the compose-service runtime. Rebuild-from-manifest is always possible: the compose file is the source of truth, the running stack is derivative. Compose is famously many right ways; over-specifying alienates a project with a defensible different shape, so v1.0.0 pins the small load-bearing set (healthchecks, secrets-as-files, restart discipline, reverse-proxy-as-artefact) and leaves everything else to project-owned ADRs.

The containerHostContract topic scope is global on this blueprint; the topic string is containerHostContract (lower camelCase, one concept per topic, no version suffix, per the round-2 rules-for-new-topics clause on the shelf registry). Standards trace clause: Docker Compose file reference AND Docker Engine install-on-Ubuntu docs per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.",
  "consequences": "Consumer blueprints that ship as containers declare capabilities: [containerHost] on their applied contract; the round-7 T-3 edge-cloudflare-tunnel reads this capability at apply-time to choose the compose-service runtime. Rebuild-from-manifest is always possible: the compose file is the source of truth, the running stack is derivative. Compose is famously many right ways; over-specifying alienates a project with a defensible different shape, so v1.0.0 pins the small load-bearing set (healthchecks, secrets-as-files, restart discipline, reverse-proxy-as-artefact) and leaves everything else to project-owned ADRs."
}
ADR-3902... T-2 reverse proxy choice: caddy default per Baz decision 19; traefik alternative for docker-label auto-discovery; none for tunnel-fronted projects (elicited) accepted

ADR-3902-platform-docker-compose-host-reverse-proxy - T-2 reverse proxy choice: caddy default per Baz decision 19; traefik alternative for docker-label auto-discovery; none for tunnel-fronted projects (elicited)

Status: accepted

Context: Compose stacks need a reverse-proxy for HTTPS termination and hostname-to-service routing. Caddy is the estate baseline (dev-01 and ops-01 already run it per Baz decision 19 on 2026-09-07 09:50Z). Traefik has a docker-label auto-discovery model some projects prefer. Some projects front their stack only with the round-7 tunnel and skip a reverse proxy inside compose.

Decision: The reverse-proxy choice is elicited via the reverseProxy parameter. The shipped default is caddy per Baz decision 19. The alternatives are traefik (for projects that want docker-label auto-discovery) and none (for projects fronted only by the round-7 tunnel). Standards trace clause: Caddy docs AND Traefik docs per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Consequences: A project applying reverseProxy=caddy gets the caddy/Caddyfile artefact and the caddy reload verb. A project applying reverseProxy=traefik gets the traefik/traefik.yaml artefact and the Traefik equivalent reload verb; docker-label auto-discovery is a project-side pattern the guide names. A project applying reverseProxy=none omits the reverse-proxy service and must apply edge-cloudflare-tunnel (T-3) so ingress terminates at the CF edge.

ADR-3904... T-2 log driver choice: journald default matching Debian 12 and Ubuntu 24.04 baseline; loki opt-in when the project runs Grafana (elicited) accepted

ADR-3904-platform-docker-compose-host-log-driver - T-2 log driver choice: journald default matching Debian 12 and Ubuntu 24.04 baseline; loki opt-in when the project runs Grafana (elicited)

Status: accepted

Context: Containers write stdout and stderr to a log driver. Debian 12 and Ubuntu 24.04 (the T-1 cloud-init baseline) ship journald. Grafana users on the estate reach for loki as a native sink. A one-choice hard-code loses either journald parity with the OS or loki when the operator runs Grafana.

Decision: The log driver is elicited via the log-driver parameter. The shipped default is journald matching the Debian 12 and Ubuntu 24.04 baselines T-1 sets up. The alternative is loki, opted into when the applying project runs Grafana. When observability-logging is applied, the compose file wires the elicited driver to that companion. Standards trace clause: generic enterprise practice.

Consequences: A project applying log-driver=journald gets the systemd-native path; the journald sink is queried via journalctl. A project applying log-driver=loki targets the Grafana loki endpoint; the observability-logging companion supplies the endpoint address. Neither choice adds a runtime npm dependency. The compose-config-lint refuses on any driver value outside the allowed set.

ADR-4001... T-3 edge ingress bridge contract: Cloudflare Tunnel as the shipped ingress-bridge shape from a cloudHost service to the CF edge (scope global, new topic edgeIngressBridge) proposed

ADR-4001-edge-cloudflare-tunnel-ingress-bridge-contract - T-3 edge ingress bridge contract: Cloudflare Tunnel as the shipped ingress-bridge shape from a cloudHost service to the CF edge (scope global, new topic edgeIngressBridge)

Status: proposed

Context: An applying project running on a Linux cloudHost needs one shipped answer to the question of how a service on that host reaches the public internet without opening origin ports. Round-7 T-3 mints the edgeIngressBridge topic on this ADR. Cloudflare Tunnel is the shipped v1.0.0 mechanism (cloudflared connector out to the CF edge; DNS route on a Cloudflare zone; ingress rules mapping public hostname to internal service URL). Every applied ingress bridge needs one project-wide answer to the edgeIngressBridge topic; a future non-Cloudflare sibling (Tailscale Funnel, Fly.io proxy) would contribute the same topic string with a different mechanism, forcing a DELIBERATE conflict the operator resolves per the round-2 conflict pattern. Standards trace clause: Cloudflare Tunnel overview and get-started documented mechanics per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Decision: The shipped v1.0.0 default is a Cloudflare Tunnel connector as the edgeIngressBridge provider. A cloudflared connector on the applying host (compose service by default when containerHost is applied per ADR-4002; systemd unit on a bare cloudHost) reads a tunnel manifest at cloudflare/tunnels/<name>.yaml and terminates ingress at the CF edge. The edgeIngressBridge topic scope is global on this blueprint; the topic string is edgeIngressBridge (lower camelCase, one concept per topic, no version suffix, per the round-2 rules-for-new-topics clause on the shelf registry). Standards trace clause: Cloudflare Tunnel overview and get-started documented mechanics per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Consequences: Consumer blueprints that expose a service publicly declare capabilities: [tunnelBridge] on their applied contract to know a bridge is in place. Composition with zeroTrustGate (edge-cloudflare-access) toggles the Access-gated ingress shape per ADR-4003. A T-3-only project (no reverse proxy) declares no 80/443 firewall rule; the tunnel is the sole path from the edge to the origin. Rebuild-from-manifest is always possible: the manifest is the source of truth, the running connector is derivative. Folding this shape into edge-cloudflare-access was rejected: Access is an authorisation gate, Tunnel is an ingress bridge; the responsibilities are distinct and one applies without the other.

ADR-4002... T-3 connector runtime: compose-service default when containerHost applied; systemd-unit alternative on bare cloudHost proposed

ADR-4002-edge-cloudflare-tunnel-connector-runtime - T-3 connector runtime: compose-service default when containerHost applied; systemd-unit alternative on bare cloudHost

Status: proposed

Context: The cloudflared connector runs in one of two supported vendor shapes: as a container image published on the cloudflared downloads page, or as a systemd unit installed via the vendor package per the cloudflared as-a-service local-configuration-file docs. An applying project running its stack under docker compose has a natural home for the connector alongside its other services (same network, same logging driver, same restart policy). An applying project running bare on the host has no compose stack and needs a systemd unit for boot ordering and journald logging. Standards trace clause: Cloudflare cloudflared as-a-service documented systemd unit per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Decision: The connector runtime is elicited via ADR-4002 with enum {compose-service, systemd-unit} and recommendedDefault compose-service. When the containerHost capability is applied (T-2 platform-docker-compose-host) the shipped default is compose-service; when the host runs bare (only T-1 applied) the operator picks systemd-unit at apply time. Standards trace clause: Cloudflare cloudflared as-a-service documented systemd unit per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Consequences: The fixture ships both variants and both pass the local probes (manifest-schema-validate, cloudflared-config-lint, aud-presence-check). A future non-Cloudflare tunnel sibling (Tailscale Funnel, Fly.io proxy) reuses the runtime enum shape but the elicit lives on that siblings own ADR (conflict-by-design on edgeIngressBridge per ADR-4001). The systemd variant carries an install caveat in the guide: the vendor package landed via apt/curl per the as-a-service docs, which is out of scope for the blueprint itself.

ADR-4003... T-3 hostname mode: access-gated when zeroTrustGate applied (ingress attaches AUD); public-hostname when absent (block omitted) proposed

ADR-4003-edge-cloudflare-tunnel-hostname-mode - T-3 hostname mode: access-gated when zeroTrustGate applied (ingress attaches AUD); public-hostname when absent (block omitted)

Status: proposed

Context: A tunnel can serve a public hostname openly (any request reaches the origin, protected only by whatever authentication the origin itself carries) or Access-gated (cloudflared refuses at the edge any request without a valid Access JWT for a named AUD, per the vendor self-hosted-public-app docs). The hostname mode is not elicited: it is DISCOVERED from the applied capability set. When zeroTrustGate is applied (edge-cloudflare-access v1.0.0), the tunnel binds the Access AUD; when it is not, the tunnel serves in public-hostname mode. Standards trace clause: Cloudflare Access self-hosted-public-app documented shape per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Decision: ADR-4003 records the hostname mode as elicited: false and discovered from applied capabilities via the sidecar rcf/blueprints/edge-cloudflare-tunnel.applied.json. When appliedCapabilities includes zeroTrustGate, every ingress rule under the tunnel manifest attaches an originRequest.access block naming the AUD; when it does not, the block is omitted. The aud-presence-check probe runs on both fixture variants and asserts the shape flips correctly. Standards trace clause: Cloudflare Access self-hosted-public-app documented shape per hetzner-round-7-spec-2026-09-07.md.

Consequences: A project that applies zeroTrustGate later inherits the Access-gated shape on the next reapply of edge-cloudflare-tunnel without a manual manifest edit; a project that removes zeroTrustGate drops to public-hostname mode explicitly. A silent drift (the sidecar keeps zeroTrustGate but the ingress loses the AUD block) is caught by aud-presence-check refusing before the shape ships. Fixture variants live under cloudflared/*/access-gated and cloudflared/*/public-hostname; the SIMULATE_AUD_DROP mutation on the gated fixture proves the refuse path.

ADR-4101... Feedback log lives at .rcf/feedback/ and is gitignored proposed

ADR-4101-feedback-store-gitignored - Feedback log lives at .rcf/feedback/ and is gitignored

Status: proposed

Context: Raw feedback entries are written before redaction runs and may hold absolute paths, hostnames and pasted error output. The store is per-clone and per-person, like rcf/.identity/ and .rcf/preflight-secrets.local.json, both already gitignored through the managed block.

Decision: The store lives under .rcf/feedback/ and is added to the managed gitignore aggregator via src/feedback/store.js:feedbackGitignoreEntry. src/setup/managed-gitignore.js:managedGitignoreEntries() imports it. rcf feedback add refuses on a project whose .gitignore does not cover the path unless --force is passed, printing the rcf doctor --fix line.

Consequences: Unredacted content cannot ride a git push, even accidentally. Existing projects need a rcf doctor --fix (or a rcf init on a fresh clone) to pick up the ignore entry. The shareable, durable record is the GitHub issue; the outbox bundle exists for cases where that record could not be made.

Alternatives considered

  • Commit rcf/feedback/ so a team can see it - Store entries under the committed rcf/ tree so any team member can browse the log.
    Not chosen because: Leaks a public-repo user's unredacted findings on the next push, which is the exact failure the redaction step exists to prevent.
