ADR-4102... Fingerprint from anchor plus symptom class; labels best-effort with a six-label bootstrap proposed

ADR-4102-fingerprint-and-labels - Fingerprint from anchor plus symptom class; labels best-effort with a six-label bootstrap

Status: proposed

Context: Same-defect folding needs a deterministic key and a triage discipline for both signed-in and outside reporters. Fingerprint from title-similarity folds wrong across unrelated findings on the same blueprint. Labels are triage handles that break for outside reporters on a public repo.

Decision: The fingerprint is sha-256(kind|targetKey|anchor|symptomClass) truncated to 12 hex characters (design section 6). Blueprint version is not part of the fingerprint. Labels are best-effort, with a fixed six-label bootstrap catalogue on every destination repo: rcf-feedback, severity:blocker, severity:major, severity:minor, area:blueprint, area:core. A repo admin runs scripts/bootstrap-feedback-labels.mjs once per destination. Title prefix ("[<slug>] " or "[rcf-lite] ") and the visible rcf-feedback-fingerprint: <fp> line stay load-bearing when labels are missing. Per-slug labels are refused (forty-plus labels to bootstrap and outside reporters cannot apply them). Operator default (pending, adjustable): Six-label bootstrap accepted as the operator default pending, adjustable. Baz can widen or narrow the catalogue at any time and library owners choose whether to add area or severity labels beyond the six on their own repos; the tool always intersects with the destination label list at submit time.

Consequences: Two agents describing the same defect on the same AC fold correctly. A defect that persists across blueprint versions produces one issue with versions in the comments. A minimal fixed label catalogue serves triage without inflating the label list per blueprint. Outside contributors on the public Stravica/rcf-lite repo still land readable issues because label absence is a soft degrade.

Alternatives considered

  • Fuzzy title matching for the fingerprint - Compute an edit-distance or token-set score across issue titles instead of the anchor input.
    Not chosen because: False folds across unrelated findings on the same blueprint and non-deterministic to test.
  • Per-slug blueprint:<slug> labels - Create one label per blueprint slug on every destination repo for finer triage.
    Not chosen because: Forty-plus labels to bootstrap on every destination and outside users still cannot apply them.

Title prefix (\"[<slug>] \" or \"[rcf-lite] \") and the visible rcf-feedback-fingerprint: <fp> line stay load-bearing when labels are missing. ADR-4103... Redaction is deterministic and rule-based; no model, no network proposed

ADR-4103-redaction-rule-based - Redaction is deterministic and rule-based; no model, no network

Status: proposed

Context: The subscription-only-LLM estate rule and the requirement that redaction be testable both point away from model-assisted redaction. Every replacement must be defensible under review; every ledger row must be reproducible from the inputs.

Decision: src/feedback/redact.js applies the eight rules of design section 5 (project root, other absolute paths, emails, non-allowlisted hosts, private IPs, secret-looking strings, operator identity, size and shape). The vendor host allowlist ships as src/feedback/redact-allowlist.json and is extended per project via rcf/feedback-settings.json:redaction.allowHosts[]. A body that still matches rule 5 on the second pass is refused, not sent.

Consequences: Redaction is testable with a fixture corpus and deterministic under review. Some over-redaction is expected (a benign name matching an entropy rule); the disclosure ledger surfaces every case so the operator can see and the agent can rewrite. The rendered output is what leaves; the stored raw entry is untouched.

Alternatives considered

  • Model-assisted redaction or summarisation - Route the body through a model to strip PII and produce a compact narrative.
    Not chosen because: Estate subscription-only rule and non-deterministic output that cannot be unit-tested.

ADR-4104... Destination is declared on library.json:issues, snapshotted on library add proposed

ADR-4104-destination-on-library - Destination is declared on library.json:issues, snapshotted on library add

Status: proposed

Context: A library that ships blueprints across many consuming projects needs one authoritative statement of where reports go. Configuring destination per consuming project means every project has to be told and every project can get it wrong independently. Derivation from the git source picks up forks and mirrors incorrectly.

Decision: library.json carries an optional issues object with repo (OWNER/REPO or HOST/OWNER/REPO for GHES) and visibility (public or private, advisory). rcf library add snapshots it onto rcf/blueprint-libraries.json:entries[] as issuesRepo and issuesVisibility. src/feedback/destination.js walks entry -> manifest -> registry -> issuesRepo, falling back to git source derivation only when the sourceRef parses as github.com/OWNER/REPO. rcf doctor gains a warn-only feedback-destinations check listing unresolved registrations.

Consequences: The library owner names where they want reports; the consuming project does not guess. Existing libraries without the field warn on doctor and route to the outbox with the publisher contact until a library update lands. Mirrored libraries no longer risk routing to the mirror.

Alternatives considered

  • Destination configured per consuming project - Put the destination in each project's rcf/feedback-settings.json.
    Not chosen because: Every WSD-using project would have to be told and get it right independently.
  • Git-source derivation as the primary route - Use the library sourceRef URL as the destination without a declared field.
    Not chosen because: A library mirrored from a fork would route reports to the fork.

ADR-4105... gh runs under the reporter ambient auth; visible identity on the public repo proposed

ADR-4105-gh-ambient-auth - gh runs under the reporter ambient auth; visible identity on the public repo

Status: proposed

Context: A relay endpoint would anonymise reporters but requires Stravica to run a service, store submissions and become the abuse surface, and is invisible to WSD for their private library. The gh CLI already carries the reporter identity and the correct permissions on every destination the reporter may reach.

Decision: Issues are created via the ambient gh CLI, under the operator own GitHub login, visibly on public and private repos alike. The tool never asks for a token, never reads GH_TOKEN or GITHUB_TOKEN itself, never spawns gh auth login. The preview names the destination and the visibility so the operator sees "under your GitHub login, on the public Stravica/rcf-lite repo" before consenting. Operator default (pending, adjustable): Visible reporter identity on Stravica/rcf-lite accepted as the operator default pending, adjustable. Baz can flip this to a relay design later without changing the CLI surface; the tool would swap gh for the relay client behind src/feedback/gh.js.

Consequences: Reporter identity is honest, which matches the operator ruling and open-source practice. The tool stays out of the credential business. Reports on the private WSD library route to WSD directly without a Stravica-side mirror.

Alternatives considered

  • A Stravica relay endpoint - Route every report through a Stravica-hosted API that anonymises before filing.
    Not chosen because: Stravica runs a service and becomes the abuse surface; invisible to WSD for their private library.

ADR-4106... Bundled entries are terminal for the ask loop proposed

ADR-4106-bundled-entries-terminal - Bundled entries are terminal for the ask loop

Status: proposed

Context: A reporter without gh, without login, or without access to a private repo would otherwise be asked every session about the same entries. Re-asking a batch that cannot land under the reporter identity nags without benefit.

Decision: When submit falls through to a bundle for an entry, that entry is marked bundled (terminal for the ask loop). rcf feedback list default (pending) hides bundled entries; the SessionStart hook does not count them; the Stop hook does not re-ask. rcf feedback submit <id> re-attempts one entry by hand once access exists.

Consequences: The operator is never nagged about the same finding. The outbox file and the printed one-line URL are what the operator uses to relay or paste the bundle. A future access change is a hand-driven re-submit, not an automatic retry.

Alternatives considered

  • Re-ask every session until submitted - Keep bundled entries pending so the next session asks again.
    Not chosen because: Nags an operator who has no path to access; a hand-driven re-submit is the correct fix.

ADR-4107... Stop is the ask event; a 15-minute quiet gate keeps the ask at a pause proposed

ADR-4107-stop-is-ask-event - Stop is the ask event; a 15-minute quiet gate keeps the ask at a pause

Status: proposed

Context: Claude Code SessionEnd output is discarded, cannot speak to the user, and shares a 1.5 second budget across hooks; Stop is the only lifecycle event that can put words in front of the user. A Stop after every rcf feedback add would interrupt the operator mid-task and read as nagging. Wrap-up cues (operator says "done", queue complete) miss most single-session users.

Decision: The ask is triggered from the Stop hook (Claude Code exit 2 + stderr; Codex JSON { decision: "block", reason }). The quiet rule (design section 3.5) requires all of: not opted out, pending entries exist, no prior asked record for this session_id, stop_hook_active is false, AND one of: entry carries askNow; the newest pending entry is older than quietMinutes (default 15) minutes; the queue-state cache reports complete or nothing actionable; the entry was carried over. quietMinutes is configurable in rcf/feedback-settings.json; --ask-now on rcf feedback add bypasses the age gate for a blocker-severity entry. Operator default (pending, adjustable): Fifteen-minute quiet gate with quietMinutes configurable and --ask-now for blocker-severity entries accepted as the operator default pending, adjustable. Baz can widen or shorten quietMinutes in rcf/feedback-settings.json at any time without a code change.

Consequences: The ask arrives at a natural pause with the exact preview text, exactly once per session_id, with a durable asked ledger that survives a crash between emit and reply. A single-session user is asked; a wrap-up-only design would miss most. quietMinutes is the single knob for anyone who finds 15 too eager or too shy.

Alternatives considered

  • Ask at the first Stop after any add - Drop the age and queue gate; the first Stop after any add asks.
    Not chosen because: Interrupts the operator mid-task and reads as nagging even though it is one question.
  • Ask on strict wrap-up cues only - Only ask when the operator says "done" or the queue reports complete.
    Not chosen because: Many single-session users are never asked.
  • Ask on SessionEnd only - Move the ask to SessionEnd so it never fires mid-session.
    Not chosen because: SessionEnd cannot speak to the user in either harness; loses single-session users entirely.

ADR-4108... Hooks live in committed harness config, installed by init and maintained by doctor proposed

ADR-4108-hooks-in-committed-config - Hooks live in committed harness config, installed by init and maintained by doctor

Status: proposed

Context: Every clone must get the same feedback ask behaviour. A user-scope hook fires on non-rcf projects and rcf init must never write outside the project. settings.local.json is per-clone and would silently skip the second developer.

Decision: rcf init merges Stop, SessionEnd and SessionStart entries into <project>/.claude/settings.json (Claude Code) and <project>/.codex/hooks.json (Codex), each pointing at npx rcf-lite feedback hook <event>. The merge respects other hooks (parse, refuse on invalid JSON, add ours only when absent, never clobber). rcf doctor gains a feedback-hooks check that reports missing-hook (fixable) and foreign-hook (a different command under our name; refused). --no-feedback-hooks on rcf init skips both writes.

Consequences: Every clone gets the ask behaviour without extra setup. doctor keeps the config honest the same way it keeps the managed block honest. Codex asks the operator to trust repo hooks the first time; RULE 17 in AGENTS.md covers the case where they decline.

Alternatives considered

  • .claude/settings.local.json per-clone - Write hooks to the per-clone settings file instead of the committed one.
    Not chosen because: The second developer never gets the hook; teams silently diverge.
  • User-scope ~/.claude hooks - Install hooks in the user home so they cover every project.
    Not chosen because: Fires on non-rcf projects; rcf init must never write outside the project.

ADR-4109... Walk ADR supersededBy and relatedAdrs at validate time, in the load-then-invert engine, not at ADR write time accepted

ADR-4109-referee-validate-adr-crosslinks - Walk ADR supersededBy and relatedAdrs at validate time, in the load-then-invert engine, not at ADR write time

Status: accepted

Context: The referee-guarantees docs page promises that `rcf define validate` proves every reference in every document resolves. The 0.27.0 walker's referential-integrity pass (`collectBrokenReferences`) walks the parent-id fields (prdId, tadId, reqId, usId, tacId, bsId) and the child-borne cross-links (fbs.acIds, fbs.contextRequirements, ts.acIds, cn.implementsAcIds / dependencies, eval.usId / acIds), but the two ADR schema fields declared for supersession semantics (`supersededBy`, `relatedAdrs`) are skipped. That leaves an honest gap between the docs promise and the tool: an ADR whose supersededBy names an id with no file on disk passes validate today. Two places are candidates for the check: (a) at ADR write time in `updateDocument` / `createDocument` (reject the write on an unresolved target), (b) at validate time in the load-then-invert walker (raise a brokenReference on the tree pass).

Decision: Walk both fields inside `collectBrokenReferences`, reusing the existing `check` helper and the `brokenReference` error kind. Two additional call blocks appended to the existing ADR loop: one for `supersededBy` (single id), one for `relatedAdrs[i]` (each entry). Neither field is required by the ADR schema, so an absent or empty field is silent; a present target must resolve to a loaded ADR of the expected kind. This matches the pattern the walker already applies to every other cross-link (fbs.contextRequirements.adrIds is the closest sibling).

Consequences: The docs-page promise holds by construction from this release. Existing WSD projects that carry stale supersession pointers will surface those failures on the next `rcf define validate` run, with the ADR file and the field named; the fix is a one-line edit or a targeted `define update` write. Choosing validate-time rather than write-time keeps the write path fast and repairable: a broken write path could refuse an operator's legitimate fix mid-repair (write-then-validate is the load-then-invert engine's contract for a reason).

Alternatives considered

  • Reject at ADR write time in createDocument / updateDocument - Add a pre-write check that refuses a write whose supersededBy or relatedAdrs entry does not resolve.
    Not chosen because: Breaks the load-then-invert repair pattern that lets `define update` fix a broken chain from the middle. A supersession that references a not-yet-created ADR (mid-refactor) would be blocked; validate is the right seam to enforce whole-tree integrity.
  • Add a separate `rcf define validate --adr-crosslinks` opt-in flag - Leave the default validate alone and expose an opt-in mode that checks the ADR cross-links.
    Not chosen because: The docs promise is universal, not opt-in. A flag-gated check is the same failure surface the referee page is being fixed to close.

      "name": "Add a separate `rcf define validate --adr-crosslinks` opt-in flag",
      "summary": "Leave the default validate alone and expose an opt-in mode that checks the ADR cross-links.",
      "reasonNotChosen": "The docs promise is universal, not opt-in. A flag-gated check is the same failure surface the referee page is being fixed to close."
    }
  ]
}
ADR-4110... Flip `rcf audit coverage` default to strict, keep `--strict` as a no-op alias, add `--mode shallow-any` as the explicit opt-out accepted

ADR-4110-referee-coverage-strict-by-default - Flip `rcf audit coverage` default to strict, keep `--strict` as a no-op alias, add `--mode shallow-any` as the explicit opt-out

Status: accepted

Context: The referee-guarantees docs page (`how-it-works/what-the-referee-guarantees`) states without qualification that a requirement counts as covered only when every acceptance criterion beneath it has a resolving Test Case, and that a stub or stale pointer fails the coverage gate exactly as a missing test does when the displayed command (`rcf audit coverage`) is run. The 0.27.0 default is shallow-any: `rcf audit coverage` prints gaps and exits 0. Strict is opt-in via `--strict`. The docs promise is therefore false against the shipped default, which was the concession made when strict landed (avoid silently failing existing CI on a version bump). The compatibility window has run: the strict flag is baked into every shipped blueprint's CI-gate posture (delivery-ci-workflows ADR-702), into the repo's own CI, into the getting-started walkthrough, and into the referee-guarantees page itself.

Decision: Flip the shipped default to strict. `--mode shallow-any` becomes the explicit opt-out (prints gaps, exits 0) so author-time exploration on a not-yet-shippable chain still has a documented home. The legacy `--strict` flag stays as a no-op alias for the new default so every existing CI invocation, blueprint README, and dogfood script keeps working byte-forward. `--mode shallow-any --strict` (or `--strict --mode shallow-any`) is a usage refusal (exit 2) so a scripted invocation cannot silently disagree with itself. The migration lands in the CHANGELOG's [Unreleased] section for the release notes.

Consequences: The referee-guarantees page's coverage sentences hold by construction from this release. Downstream projects on 0.27.0 that ran the plain `rcf audit coverage` and treated its exit code as passing will see that command exit 4 on the same tree; the fix is either to close the coverage gap or to run `rcf audit coverage --mode shallow-any` when the intent is a printed gap report rather than a gate. Existing `rcf audit coverage --strict` invocations (the shipped blueprints' CI gates, the repo's own CI, downstream projects' pipelines) keep working. The CHANGELOG entry names the migration so a version bumper is not surprised.

Alternatives considered

  • Rename the current default: `--mode` required, no default - Require callers to name their mode explicitly; refuse the bare command until a mode is passed.
    Not chosen because: Breaks every existing invocation, blueprint, and CI dogfood; the referee-guarantees page itself would need a mode-name for the command it displays. Strict-by-default with a shallow-any opt-out satisfies the docs promise with no rewrite of the shipped invocations.
  • Deprecate --strict; emit a warn line under the new default - Print a deprecation warning when --strict is passed so callers move to the new default explicitly.
    Not chosen because: Every shipped blueprint's CI-gate posture is `rcf audit coverage --strict`; a deprecation line at every CI run is noise that hides the report, not a helpful nudge. --strict is a no-op alias, not a warning surface.

ADR-4111... finalise refuses on UI-BASELINE-UNMET / BROWSER-VERIFICATION-MISSING / SCOPE-MISMATCH with no sister opt-out accepted

ADR-4111-referee-finalise-refusals - finalise refuses on UI-BASELINE-UNMET / BROWSER-VERIFICATION-MISSING / SCOPE-MISMATCH with no sister opt-out

Status: accepted

Context: The referee-guarantees docs page names three per-AC verdicts that finalise refuses on top of the 0.7.0 MOCK-ONLY / BLOCKED-BY-DECLARATION and rcf-eval-node EVAL-MISSING / EVAL-BELOW-THRESHOLD refusals: UI-BASELINE-UNMET (docs claim C-28; a block-severity probe-pack failure aggregates into the same verdict, C-36), BROWSER-VERIFICATION-MISSING (C-29) and SCOPE-MISMATCH (C-30). The verdict layer already emits all three (see `uiPerAcVerdict` and `scopePerAcVerdict` in `src/verify/verdict/index.js`); the aggregator in `src/browser-verify/manifest-writer.js` produces UI-BASELINE-UNMET for a block-severity probe-pack failure. The gap is at finalise: the 0.27.0 CLI branched on MOCK-ONLY / EVAL but not on the three new verdicts, so a report that passed the top-level verdict with a UI-BASELINE-UNMET on a per-AC verdict silently promoted. The docs page also names two sister opt-outs (--ship-without-verified, --ship-without-eval) for the existing refusals; it does NOT spell an opt-out for the three new verdicts.

Decision: Refuse promotion (exit 4) on any of the three per-AC verdicts, in the order UI-BASELINE-UNMET, BROWSER-VERIFICATION-MISSING, SCOPE-MISMATCH, appended after the EVAL refusal branch in finalise.js. No --ship-without-* opt-out is added for these three: the docs page names none, and the underlying failures (broken UI baseline, missing browser check, scope-mismatched TC) are exactly the shape the referee is chartered to refuse. If a project needs to ship anyway, the fix is on the tree (widen the TC, land the browser-verify record, fix the baseline). Each refusal message names the referee-guarantees claim ids so a downstream reader can trace back to the docs promise.

Consequences: The referee-guarantees page's three sentences hold by construction. Verify reports on existing WSD projects that already emit these verdicts will now fail finalise where they previously silently promoted; that is the point. Adding a --ship-without-* opt-out later remains open (would follow the ship-without-verified shape with a schema addition for the new verdict enum), but is not landed here because the docs page has not named one and the failure classes are the kind that should be fixed on the tree, not acked away.

Alternatives considered

  • Add a single --ship-without-referee flag for all three - Introduce a catch-all acknowledgement flag that acks any of the three new verdicts and records the ack on the manifest under a new shipWithoutRefereeChecks[] section.
    Not chosen because: Requires a rcf-schemas manifest bump (a new shipWithoutRefereeChecksRecord shape), the docs page has not spelled such an opt-out, and the failure classes (broken baseline, missing browser check, scope mismatch) are not the kind that operators legitimately ship over. Refusing without an opt-out matches the docs promise as written.

ADR-4112... Gate the manual verified override behind --acknowledge-verified-override; add a default-branch precondition to finalise with --allow-pre-merge as the opt-out accepted

ADR-4112-referee-finalise-verified-invariant - Gate the manual verified override behind --acknowledge-verified-override; add a default-branch precondition to finalise with --allow-pre-merge as the opt-out

Status: accepted

Context: The referee-guarantees docs page promises that `rcf build finalise` is the only path to `verified` (docs claim C-22) and that a chain that says `verified` traces to an actual post-merge runtime check by construction (C-26). Two 0.27.0 gaps break those promises: (a) `rcf define update <fbs> --set executionStatus=verified` writes the value directly through the writer, bypassing finalise entirely, and (b) finalise itself has no merge-state precondition, so a mid-branch dev-loop run can stamp verified against a localhost URL. The docs sentence explicitly says both are on the 0.28.0 landing plan: 'The next release removes the manual override and adds the merge-state precondition, so once shipped, a chain that says verified traces to an actual post-merge runtime check by construction.' Two constraints shape the fix: (1) the manifest schema admits `verified` as a valid executionStatus so finalise itself can write it, and (2) the escalation clause on this dispatch: if the fix breaks existing WSD projects, land it behind a flag whose default matches the docs promise.

Decision: Two symmetric refusals, each with a documented escape flag. (a) The writer refuses FBS.executionStatus=verified when `options.allowVerifiedOverride` is not true; finalise's own updateDocument call passes the flag through, and `rcf define update` exposes `--acknowledge-verified-override` for the deliberate manual override (a logged operator decision). (b) Finalise spawns `git rev-parse --abbrev-ref HEAD` just before the executionStatus write and refuses (exit 4) when the branch is not one of {main, master}; `--allow-pre-merge` is the deliberate pre-merge dry-run opt-out, and the decision is logged on stdout so the operator sees it. Absent a git checkout (bare tarball deploy, container ephemeral CWD), the check degrades to a warn line rather than a hard fail so legitimate non-git deploys are not refused by a git-shape check.

Consequences: Both docs sentences hold by default from this release. Downstream projects that ran `rcf define update <fbs> --set executionStatus=verified` for a repair scenario keep the escape valve through the new flag; downstream projects that ran finalise on a feature branch for a dev-loop dry run keep the escape valve through --allow-pre-merge. The refusal messages and the log lines name the referee-guarantees claim ids so a downstream reader can trace the behaviour to the docs promise it enforces. The two default-branch names (main, master) are hard-coded rather than read from the git remote's symbolic ref; projects on a non-default trunk name either rename to a listed name or run --allow-pre-merge every time (unusual in modern repos).

Alternatives considered

  • Remove the manual override entirely (no --acknowledge-verified-override flag) - Refuse FBS.executionStatus=verified through the writer with no escape flag; force every verified write through finalise.
    Not chosen because: Escalation clause: existing WSD projects may need a manual repair escape (e.g. a finalise gate that promoted then a partial rollback that needs the state re-stamped). A hard removal invalidates that repair path; the flag preserves it with a logged, deliberate operator decision.
  • Merge-state check reads the git remote's symbolic ref for the default branch - Instead of hard-coding {main, master}, run `git symbolic-ref refs/remotes/origin/HEAD` and use its value as the default trunk name.
    Not chosen because: Adds a network round-trip on every finalise, fails offline, and depends on the remote's ref being set (many test scaffolds do not set it). The small hard-coded list matches what git init and every hosted git provider default to today; projects on an unusual trunk name pass --allow-pre-merge every time or rename to a listed name.
  • Verify the merge with git merge-base HEAD origin/main - Instead of a branch-name check, verify the current commit is an ancestor of origin/main.
    Not chosen because: Requires the operator to `git fetch` before finalise (a silent staleness bug otherwise), depends on the remote name and is slower. The branch-name check is a proxy that catches the common failure (finalise on a feature branch) without a network hop.

ADR-4120... Delta detection hashes the parsed document under canonical JSON, at standalone-document granularity accepted

ADR-4120-canonical-json-hashing - Delta detection hashes the parsed document under canonical JSON, at standalone-document granularity

Status: accepted

Context: The DEFINE workflow proposal (2026-09-22 v3, section 2.1) has to pick both a hashing scheme and a granularity for docHashes on the freeze record. Two choices matter and are named as residual (proposal section 2 penultimate paragraph): raw bytes versus the parsed canonical form, and criterion-level versus document-level. Raw bytes are the smallest amount of code (one hash per file read); the parsed form costs one canonicalise per document per read (milliseconds at 700 criteria). Criterion granularity gives a finer delta; document granularity keeps the model small and lets git supply the criterion-level diff. Both choices had to be recorded because the detection model is what every later slice (readiness, freeze, bundle, viewer) reads.

Decision: Hash the parsed document under canonical JSON: keys sorted recursively, no whitespace, JSON.stringify escaping. Compute the tree hash as SHA-256 over the sorted (id, docHash) pairs canonically encoded. The docHashes map has one entry per standalone document the walker exposes on tree.byId (PRD, TAD, BS, REQ, US, TAC, ADR, FBS, TS, CN, EVAL) plus one ledger:<name> entry per sidecar the caller passes; inline AC and TC ride inside their parent's hash. Granularity for the delta list is the standalone document.

Consequences: A hand reformat of a document (rewritten by rcf define update, opened in an editor and re-saved) does not surface as a change, which is what an operator expects. An edit to a criterion surfaces as its owning story changed; Readiness renders the criterion-level diff by reading the frozen story out of git (proposal section 2.2). The cost is one canonicalise per document per read; at the backstory scale of 700 criteria that is milliseconds and is only paid on readiness / freeze / bundle --next reads. If document granularity turns out too coarse in practice, ADR replacement or schemas 0.7's criterion-hash extension is the migration path; the change would not affect the wire shape of computeDelta because inline granularity would simply expand tree.byId, not the return shape.

Alternatives considered

  • Hash the raw file bytes - SHA-256 over readFile output directly; skip canonical JSON entirely.
    Not chosen because: A CLI edit that rewrites the file (rcf define update reserialises the object every write) would report drift on a file it did not semantically touch. The operator would learn to ignore the delta list, which is the one signal the freeze exists to give.
  • Criterion granularity: one docHash per AC / TC on top of the document ones - Add inline-AC and inline-TC entries to docHashes so an edit to AC-207-4 shows in the delta at criterion granularity.
    Not chosen because: Doubles the size of docHashes for no readiness improvement: Readiness already renders the criterion-level diff by reading the frozen story from git. The size cost is real (a backstory tree has 700 criteria plus 40 stories); the render cost is not.
  • Hash the pretty-printed JSON body the writer produced - Hash JSON.stringify(doc, null, 2) plus a trailing newline; the same bytes the writer wrote.
    Not chosen because: Whitespace-only reformats (a hand edit that reorders keys or drops a trailing newline) then surface as changes. Canonical hashing is the same code with the whitespace stripped and the keys sorted; the operator sees fewer false-positive deltas.

ADR-4121... Ledgers as rcf-lite-owned sidecars under rcf/define/ with a local schema; promote to manifest records at schemas 0.7 accepted

ADR-4121-define-sidecars - Ledgers as rcf-lite-owned sidecars under rcf/define/ with a local schema; promote to manifest records at schemas 0.7

Status: accepted

Context: The DEFINE proposal (2026-09-22 v3, section 2.5 and decision 5) needs a place to put four things the workflow reads and writes but the shared schema does not yet know about: brief statements (D1), decisions (D7), (concern, REQ) dispositions (D5), probe findings (D6). @stravica-ai/rcf-schemas 0.6.3 has no manifest.ledgers[] shape and adding one is a schema-package bump; the train's non-goal (train-context: 'no schema change') is to ship the workflow without touching @stravica-ai/rcf-schemas. Precedent already exists in this codebase: .rcf/preflight-secrets.local.json is an rcf-lite-owned file outside the shared schema; the loader reads only its named collection directories, so a directory the walker was not told about is invisible.

Decision: Ledgers live under rcf/define/, one JSON file each (brief-ledger.json, decisions-ledger.json, concern-ledger.json, probe-ledger.json), validated by a local schema inside src/define/ledgers.js. The freeze record sits at rcf/define/freeze.json under the same directory. rcf-lite owns the shape until @stravica-ai/rcf-schemas 0.7, at which point the sidecars promote to a manifest.freeze and manifest.ledgers[] records and the local schema is retired. The walker never reads rcf/define/ (src/core/store/loader.js's subdirFor returns null for anything not in its child-kind list), and a walker-invisibility invariant test proves it stays that way.

Consequences: A DEFINE change lands with no @stravica-ai/rcf-schemas bump: the train ships as 0.29.0 against the shipped 0.6.3 schema. The sidecars are committed alongside the rest of the rcf tree (they carry durable state: the freeze hash, brief statement ids, resolved decisions), so git supplies the history the proposal section 2.1 relies on. Second source of truth is the honest downside: until schemas 0.7 there are two places the DEFINE workflow reads (the shared tree and rcf/define/); the promotion path documented in the proposal (section 5.3) is straightforward because the local shapes were designed to line up with the manifest.freeze and manifest.ledgers[] fields the schema promotion adds. If schemas 0.7 slips past the 0.30 train, the sidecars keep working: the local schema is the contract every DEFINE gate consumes.

Alternatives considered

  • Land the manifest.freeze and manifest.ledgers[] records at schemas 0.6.4 now - Bump @stravica-ai/rcf-schemas to 0.6.4 as part of this train; add manifest.freeze and manifest.ledgers[] optional records; write to the manifest instead of a sidecar.
    Not chosen because: The train-context ('no schema change') is a deliberate constraint on this train, ratified 2026-09-22, so the workflow can ship without another WSD-side schema round trip. Schemas 0.7 is on the roadmap for the 0.30 train; landing the sidecar first proves the shape at zero schema cost, then the promotion carries the same fields.
  • One combined ledger file (rcf/define/ledger.json) with four sections - Collapse the four ledgers into one file with four top-level keys; the CLI still gates on the name.
    Not chosen because: The four ledgers grow independently (a probe-heavy pass writes ten probes with no decisions changed) and merge conflicts on a shared file would surface constantly. Four files with distinct id sequences is the cheaper long-term shape, and it lines up with the four manifest.ledgers[] records schemas 0.7 is expected to add.
  • Sidecars under .rcf/ (like preflight-secrets.local.json) - Put the four ledgers under .rcf/ so they inherit the preflight-secrets convention.
    Not chosen because: The preflight sidecar is gitignored on purpose (credential name-metadata). DEFINE ledgers hold durable state the workflow re-reads on every gate; they must be committed. rcf/define/ keeps them visible to the operator, alongside the tree they annotate.

ADR-4122... Blocking-vs-warn-with-ack per stage; D4 per-class opt-out reuses manifest.baselineAcOptOuts[] accepted

ADR-4122-define-gates-blocking-and-optout - Blocking-vs-warn-with-ack per stage; D4 per-class opt-out reuses manifest.baselineAcOptOuts[]

Status: accepted

Context: The DEFINE workflow proposal (2026-09-22 v3, section 3.2, decision 2) blocks where the data exists and warns-with-acknowledgement for D3, D5, D6 until the release that lands the 0.30 (renumbered from 0.31 per Baz 2026-09-24) contradiction-lite, unsatisfiable-lite, template parser and probe runner. Proposal section 3.2 also says D4's failure and must-not floors accept a 'reasoned opt-out per class, as the baseline ledger works (#239)'. The train has to decide whether the D4 opt-out reuses the existing manifest.baselineAcOptOuts[] machinery (nextOptOutId, composeOptOutRecord under src/req-baseline/opt-out.js, boo-YYYY-MM-DD-NNN ids) or gets a new sidecar under rcf/define/. Second decision that had to be recorded because slice 2's gates read it and slice 3's freeze verb writes it: how does the freeze record acknowledge a warn-with-ack gate?

Decision: Blocking in 0.29.0: D1 (define.brief), D2 (define.skeleton), D4 floors (define.stories), D7 (define.decisions), D8 (define.freeze). Warn-with-ack in 0.29.0: D3 (define.shapes), D5 (define.crosscut), D6 (define.consistency). Blocking-vs-warn-with-ack is a stage property, hard-coded in src/query/gates.js. The state fold: a stage is 'passed' when every check.ok is true; 'failing' otherwise. For D3/D5/D6 the fold flips to 'acknowledged' when the freeze record's gates[<gate>] entry names state 'acknowledged' AND at.hash === currentTreeHash. D4 per-class opt-outs reuse manifest.baselineAcOptOuts[]: baselineKey is 'defineD4:failure' or 'defineD4:mustNot'; scope is 'req' (opt-out applies to every US whose reqId matches the record's reqId) or 'project' (applies tree-wide). Slice-3 writes acknowledgements via the freeze verb; the write path is out of scope for slice 2. The opt-out records are authored by an operator through the existing req-baseline surface (or, in slice 3, an optional --optout flag on freeze); slice 2 only reads them.

Consequences: One place to author opt-outs (the existing baselineAcOptOuts array), one place to read them (the same array). No new sidecar until D4's class opt-outs mature (schemas 0.7 will move them if the shape stabilises). The freeze record's gates map becomes the single source of truth for acknowledgements, which is what slice-3's freeze verb writes and every consumer reads. The honest downside: the baselineKey field is loosely typed (free-string convention rather than an enum), so a typo lands silently (the D4 gate simply does not honour the opt-out). Mitigation: the checker prints a stderr [warn] when it sees a record with a baselineKey starting with 'defineD4:' but not matching the two known values, and the CLI docs (slice 3 / slice 6) list the accepted keys. If the shape ever needs to move, existing records can be migrated by rewriting the manifest under the same array without a schema change.

Alternatives considered

  • New sidecar rcf/define/class-optout-ledger.json for D4 per-class opt-outs - Fifth sidecar under rcf/define/ with entries { id, scope, reqId?, usId?, class: 'failure'|'mustNot', reason, addedAt }; add --class flag to rcf define ledger.
    Not chosen because: Adds a fifth sidecar to a proposal (decision 5) that ratified four. Proposal section 3.2 D4 explicitly says 'as the baseline ledger works (#239)', pointing at the existing surface. A fifth ledger costs a schema, a CLI branch and a walker-invisibility test for zero gain over reusing the shape.
  • Block D3, D5, D6 in 0.29.0 (drop warn-with-ack) - Every stage blocks; --ack is not a thing until 0.30.
    Not chosen because: Baz's decision 2 ratifies warn-with-ack for D3/D5/D6 until the template parser, catalogue and scans land. Blocking on cheap presence-only checks (an unknown interface kind, or a probe finding still open) refuses freezes on tree state that 0.30's richer checks would tolerate; the acknowledgement channel is what lets an operator move without inventing the check they need is not there.
  • Encode blocking-vs-warn-with-ack on each check rather than on the stage - Every check[i] carries a policy tag; the fold reads the tags rather than the stage.
    Not chosen because: The proposal is stage-scoped, not check-scoped. Per-check policy tags land as future noise for zero present gain: today every check inside a stage shares a policy. If a stage grows a check with a different policy the fold moves back to per-stage anyway (a 'failing' check on any policy is still 'failing' in the current model).

ADR-4123... Readiness is one computed object; no stored stage state, no stored 'stale' accepted

ADR-4123-readiness-single-object - Readiness is one computed object; no stored stage state, no stored 'stale'

Status: accepted

Context: The DEFINE workflow proposal (2026-09-22 v3, section 2.4, section 6, decision 4) is explicit that the CLI and the viewer tab render the same object so they cannot disagree, and that stage state is one of passed | failing | acknowledged | notApplicable with no 'stale' and no 'notStarted' because nothing is stored: every chip is the truth at the moment of the read. The Product Map (PR #238) precedent already ships this pattern for a related surface. Slice 2 has to pick both the computation shape (one pass or many; where the impact fan-out sits) and the storage shape (nothing stored, or a small cache in the freeze record).

Decision: computeReadiness returns one plain-data object per call over the tree, the freeze record and the four ledgers; nothing is stored between calls, and no per-stage 'stale' flag exists. The stage state is a pure fold over the checks[] of that stage: 'passed' when every check.ok is true, 'failing' otherwise, unless the stage is one of the three warn-with-ack stages and the freeze record's gates[<gate>] entry names 'acknowledged' at the current tree hash. The CLI (rcf define readiness) prints the object; slice-5's viewer renders the same JSON envelope over the existing tab wire (proposal section 6.3). runWithAdmissibilityGate wraps the CLI's producer, matching the ruleset toolScope { traceabilityAndQueryTools: true } switch; slice 2 records this decision because the wrap changes the shipping exit path. On refuse the wrap runs first (so the ruleset toolScope guard is honoured, NV-BL-SR-03 addendum), then the readiness compute runs anyway and the CLI prints an informational [warn] on stderr naming the refusal, because readiness is a diagnostic and refusing to report which stage blocks is the opposite of what the verb exists to do; the process still exits 0 (or the --check <stage> code) and never exits 4 solely on refuse.

Consequences: One shape, two renderers: whatever the CLI prints, the viewer prints. Absence of stored state means Readiness is stateless: git carries the history, the freeze record carries the acknowledgements, everything else is derived. The compute cost is one canonicalise per document per read (already ratified in ADR-4120) plus one computeImpact per delta id, which on the dogfood chain (~700 documents, ~30 delta ids on a small feature) is measured in single-digit seconds. If the compute ever costs too much, the mitigation is a per-render cache in the CLI or the viewer (not in the freeze record), so the shape stays the same. Honest downside: the whole-tree unfrozen case (no freeze record; every doc is 'added') computes computeImpact over every id, which on very large trees may be quadratic in fan-out size. Slice 2 mitigates by skipping the per-id fan-out when the delta is the whole tree (the delta IS the fan-out), and the CLI prints wall time so an operator can spot a regression before it becomes a defect.

Alternatives considered

  • Cache the last stage[] under freeze.gates[]; only re-run gates whose delta touches their scope - Store per-stage checks + fold under freeze.gates[]; readiness reads the cache and only re-runs gates the delta invalidates.
    Not chosen because: Two sources of truth: the tree and the cache. Every operator correction to a story would have to invalidate the cache correctly, and any bug in the invalidation would show up as a false green. Proposal section 2.4 explicitly rules this out: 'no stale, no not-started'. Recompute is cheap enough not to earn the complexity.
  • Skip runWithAdmissibilityGate on the readiness verb - Readiness is a diagnostic; run it even when admissibility refuses so the operator can see what to fix.
    Not chosen because: The ruleset toolScope switch { traceabilityAndQueryTools: true } is a runtime-read guard (NV-BL-SR-03 addendum) and matches every other query verb's expected posture; skipping it would be an exception the checker cannot see. Slice 2 wraps the producer; a future train can add an explicit --show-anyway flag if the diagnostic case wins the argument, and record it as an ADR replacement.
  • Compute stages fully in parallel with Promise.all - Every stage check runs in parallel via Promise.all against a shared context.
    Not chosen because: The gate check functions are pure and CPU-bound (no I/O); Promise.all does not parallelise CPU on Node without workers, and worker-thread overhead is far larger than the compute cost. Sequential composition is honest about what the code does.

ADR-4124... rcf define freeze refuses on any failing stage and only D3/D5/D6 accept an --ack override accepted

ADR-4124-define-freeze-verb - rcf define freeze refuses on any failing stage and only D3/D5/D6 accept an --ack override

Status: accepted

Context: Proposal 2026-09-22 v3 section 2.5 defines the freeze verb as the only close verb: it runs readiness, refuses on any failing gate, accepts --ack <gate> --reason on the three warn-first gates, and writes the freeze record. Section 3.2 lists five blocking gates in 0.29.0 (D1, D2, D4 floors, D7, D8) and three warn-with-ack gates (D3, D5, D6). Baz ruling 2026-09-24 (Baz decision 2 in section 9): warn-with-ack ack is accepted only on D3 / D5 / D6, never on the blocking gates. Slice 3 has to pick (a) whether ack on a non-warn gate is a usage refusal or a runtime refusal; (b) whether the freeze verb re-runs readiness after ack (or applies acks in-memory); (c) whether admissibility refusal counts as a freeze refusal or a warning. Slice 1 shipped a freeze-record writer with override as an optional nullable field, and the P3 review note flagged the local-schema mismatch (JSDoc said required-nullable, validator said optional).

Decision: The freeze verb refuses (exit 4) on any stage state 'failing' after applying --ack acknowledgements in-memory. --ack is a compile-time contract: unknown gate names (anything outside define.shapes / define.crosscut / define.consistency and their aliases) are usage refusals (exit 2), and every --ack must be paired with a matching --reason (exit 2 on mismatched arities). Acknowledgements are applied to an in-memory freeze.gates map keyed by gate id, and each warn-with-ack stage's state is recomputed with the same fold gates.js foldState uses (WARN_WITH_ACK + at.hash === currentTreeHash). freeze then writes the freeze record with these acknowledgements persisted so slice 5's viewer and a future computeReadiness call render the stage as 'acknowledged' at that hash. Admissibility refusal is informational (ADR-4123 carried): the wrap runs first so the ruleset toolScope guard is honoured, and on refuse the CLI prints a stderr [warn] and the freeze compute continues. The freeze verb never exits 4 solely for a refused-admissibility verdict. Slice 3 also fixes the slice-1 P3 by making validateFreezeRecord require override as a nullable field, and by making saveFreezeRecord always stamp override: null on a fresh freeze so the schema surface is single-sourced before slice 4 reads it. Older records that omit the key are tolerated by loadFreezeRecord defaulting to null on read.

Consequences: One verb, one contract, one exit code path. Operators cannot silently ack a blocking gate: the ack fails at parseArgs time with a message naming the accepted set, which is easier to reason about than a runtime refusal deep in the compute. The in-memory ack recomputation keeps the write path a pure function of the tree + the acks: nothing partial is written if the compute later rejects. Persisted acks show up on the next readiness run because the freeze.gates entry stores { state: 'acknowledged', at: { hash, at, reason } } and gates.js folds against the current tree hash. Honest downside: an operator who acks a warn-with-ack gate and then edits the tree without re-freezing sees the ack disappear on the next readiness run (the hash changed, so foldState drops back to 'failing'). This matches proposal section 2.5 ('closing a change is freezing again') and is the same posture the readiness verb has today. Override-nullable-required means every existing freeze fixture (in tests, in dogfood chains) is expected to carry override: null; the loader tolerates a missing key on read (fills in null) so older records survive, but writing a record without override is a validator failure. The double-dash hygiene is a one-line change per file with a targeted golden-fixture update.

Alternatives considered

  • Accept --ack on any gate; refuse at runtime with a message - Let --ack take any gate name; the freeze compute checks the ack list against the warn-with-ack set and exits 4 with an error when a blocking gate is acked.
    Not chosen because: Slower feedback (parseArgs is instant, the readiness compute takes seconds on a large tree), and it lets an ack land in the ack map that will never be honoured. A usage refusal at parseArgs time matches the rest of the CLI's contract (unknown --check gates are refused there too).
  • Re-run computeReadiness after applying acks - Persist an intermediate freeze record with the acks, re-run computeReadiness against it, decide the exit code from the second run.
    Not chosen because: Two writes and two computes; the second compute reads the same tree so the only difference is the freeze.gates map. Folding in-memory with gates.js foldState is one function call and matches what a slice-5 viewer would render if it were doing the same thing.
  • Refuse the freeze on refused-admissibility - Treat a refused-admissibility verdict as a fatal freeze failure; exit 4 with the refusal envelope on stderr.
    Not chosen because: ADR-4123 already ruled that readiness is a diagnostic and refuses to hide the block. The freeze verb is the write half of the same object; refusing the freeze solely because admissibility refused means an operator with a valid freezeable tree cannot close the change until the admissibility rules unblock. The refusal is still surfaced as a [warn] on stderr so it is not silent.

ADR-4126... Intent-complete is a persona cut, computed, never recorded accepted

ADR-4126-persona-tagged-blockers-two-levels - Intent-complete is a persona cut, computed, never recorded

Status: accepted

Context: WSD needs a product-owner exit from DEFINE that a delivery stream can pick up without a hand-over meeting. Dex proposed early-stage gates; the design-spec review (2026-10-01) walked a middle path. D2 and D4 each hold both PO and engineer checks today; a single-persona tag per check would misread both. Operators also need a way to pre-populate shapes at L1 without those shapes reading as the engineer's finished work. The gate table has 20 checks in 0.29.0; two are heterogeneous and one is missing. The train is 4.5 days across three PRs; PR A owns the compute.

Decision: Every gate check in src/query/gates.js declares an owning persona (productOwner | engineer) via a code-side CHECK_PERSONA map and a one-sentence CHECK_QUESTION heading in the persona's register. The two heterogeneous checks are split: skeleton:reqFields becomes skeleton:reqIntent (productOwner: description + domain) + skeleton:reqShape (engineer: shapeClassification.shapes); decisions:allAnswered becomes decisions:wellFormed (productOwner: enumerated per #241 format) + decisions:allAnswered (engineer: zero open). A new D3 check shapes:draftSettled fails every interface whose description still carries the leading [draft] marker, so an L1-pre-populated interface is distinguishable from a settled one; shapes:tacHasInterface counts a draft as present, and shapes:kindVocabulary applies to drafts. L1 intent-complete is 'every productOwner check ok across every stage', computed by computeReadiness and folded into readiness.levels.intentComplete alongside the existing freezeable-equivalent readiness.levels.readyToBuild. Nothing is written; both levels fall out of stages[].checks[] on every read. The notApplicable placeholder (stage:<D>:scope) carries a per-stage fallback persona (STAGE_FALLBACK_PERSONA map) so every check has a persona for the table test and downstream renderers; the placeholder is always ok so it never affects a level. There is no either / shared / both persona; a check that would need both is split instead. Per-item persona override is not introduced; a failing item inherits its check's persona. Open decisions do not block L1 in 0.29.0: an enumerated decision with a default is enough for an engineer to proceed (Baz direction doc, open question 1 answered Dave-recommended). The [draft] marker lives on TAC.interfaces[].description only in 0.29.0, mirroring decision 6's AC-class bracket convention; rcf-schemas 0.6.3 is untouched and the marker migrates with AC.kind to a structured field at schemas 0.7.

Consequences: One ladder, two verdicts. Intent-complete is the ticket artefact a delivery stream reads from `rcf define readiness --level intent --json`; it is not recorded, so no second register of truth and nothing to invalidate on tree change. The persona split in gates.js is one map plus two straightforward loops (reqIntent / reqShape each evaluates every REQ independently; wellFormed / allAnswered each loop decisionEntries); every existing test except the two renamed checks keeps passing unchanged, and the dogfood tree reports two extra findings on reqIntent that were previously masked by the first-failure continue (true findings, not regressions). The notApplicable placeholder carrying a persona is a small schema surface addition that keeps the per-check vocabulary total true. The [draft] marker as a text convention is the same posture AC class carries today (decision 6); the migration cost at schemas 0.7 is one more lift. L1 pre-population is explicit: the L1 agent writes [draft] interfaces as it learns entities and routes from the brief, which makes shapes:tacHasInterface pass earlier for the engineer and leaves shapes:draftSettled as the honest list of what the engineer has yet to own. L2 draft handling is unchanged: a failing shapes:draftSettled keeps D3 failing unless acknowledged at the current hash through the existing --ack define.shapes path (0.29.0 warn-with-ack posture; step 4 makes D3 bite). The levels object cannot disagree with the CLI or the Readiness tab because all three render from the same computeReadiness output. The CLI flags that expose levels (--level, --persona) and the viewer tab land in PRs B and C respectively; this ADR only covers the compute.

Alternatives considered

  • Stage-prefix persona (every check on D1/D2/D4/D7 is productOwner; D3/D5/D6/D8 is engineer) - Pin persona by stage, skip the per-check tag; no splits.
    Not chosen because: Blocks the PO on skeleton:tadPersistence (data stores) and skeleton:deployAdr (which hosting), both engineering decisions. Also passes with unresolved brief statements under an engineer-only D5 even though resolution is a PO question. The per-check map is the source of truth because the owner is a property of the rule, not of the stage.
  • Recorded L1 (freeze-at-intent) - Write an intent-complete freeze record parallel to the build freeze, with its own hash and ledger.
    Not chosen because: Reintroduces stored state the detection model (REQ-172) removed. Two freeze records on one tree are two chances for them to disagree, and the delivery stream's artefact is already the --json output at a tree hash. L1 is a verdict, not a commit.
  • either / shared / both persona value - Allow a check to be owned by both personas when it reads both ways.
    Not chosen because: Hides whose question it is, which was the point of the tag. A heterogeneous check is almost always two checks under one name; splitting is clearer and cheap.
  • [draft] on a new TAC.interfaces[].status field instead of description - Introduce a structured status enum on the interface shape.
    Not chosen because: Schema change for one piece of 0.29.0 metadata; AC class already lives on description as a bracket prefix (decision 6); the two migrate together at schemas 0.7. The 0.29.0 cost is one regex.
  • Per-item persona override on failing[] - Let a failing { id, why } carry its own persona so one check can fail into both personas.
    Not chosen because: A failing item carries no new information its check does not already carry; the operator reads the question heading, not the item. Keeps the API surface narrower and avoids forcing every consumer to fold two persona fields.

ADR-4127... Readiness is tab 1 always and renders the same object as the CLI; the register orders persona groups and never hides one accepted

ADR-4127-readiness-tab-order-and-register - Readiness is tab 1 always and renders the same object as the CLI; the register orders persona groups and never hides one

Status: accepted

Context: DEFINE step 2 (0.29.0) exposes two verdicts on the one readiness ladder. The CLI prints them (PR B); the viewer must carry the same object so the two surfaces cannot disagree. Overview today is just the PRD body (phase 3.6 dropped the diagram), so it never earns first-tab status, and operators asked for a landing surface that leads with 'can I build and whose questions stand in the way'. The persona register from profile.md orders the CLI text report; the tab must honour the same register without ever hiding the non-register group.

Decision: Readiness is tab 1 of the HTML review surface, always, and renders the computeReadiness result directly. The former Overview tab is renamed PRD with no content change; the data-tab=overview and id=tab-overview identifiers are preserved so every existing `#tab-overview` hash link still resolves. The viewer's renderer is pure: it reads the result object and the profile text and emits HTML; it never recomputes readiness or hits disk. The profile register from pickRegister orders the persona groups (productOwner-first by default; engineer-first when the register says engineer; unstated prints the pair in default order). The non-register group is always rendered with its count visible; collapsed by default, never omitted from the DOM. The Freeze now control is enabled iff levels.readyToBuild.ok; disabled, it names the failing gates from levels.readyToBuild.blockedBy. There is no intent-complete button at L1 (nothing to record; ADR-4126). The 0.29.0 diff component in the delta list is document-level only; criterion-level before-and-after is deferred to the UX review (open question 7 of the step 2 spec).

Consequences: One readiness object renders three ways (CLI text, CLI JSON, viewer tab) with no second register of truth; AC-18001-7 asserts the identity by walking the rendered anchors and matching them to the --json for the same tree hash. The Overview-to-PRD rename is cosmetic for hash routing and content; existing anchors keep working. Shared components land once, pay down the drift between tabs, and are additive on the Product Map and Requirements tabs in 0.29.0 (re-pointing is a follow-up where the swap is not mechanical). Deferring the criterion-level diff keeps PR C small and leaves the AC-class before-and-after question to the UX review it belongs to.

Alternatives considered

  • Readiness as the fifth tab, Overview stays first - Keep Overview as the landing tab and add Readiness at the end.
    Not chosen because: Overview is one block today (the PRD body); it does not earn the landing. Making an operator click to see the verdict is friction for the thing the surface exists to answer.
  • Rename to data-tab=prd and migrate hash anchors - Rename both the label and the identifier so the surface reads consistently.
    Not chosen because: Every existing `#tab-overview` link in documents and in commit messages breaks. The label is for humans; the identifier is for links. Keeping the identifier is cheaper than migrating every link.
  • Hide the non-register persona group - When the register is productOwner, omit the engineer group from the DOM entirely (and vice versa).
    Not chosen because: AC-18001-5 is must-not for a reason: hiding a persona breaks the parity the CLI --json offers. The tab is a diagnostic, not a filter; the collapse-with-count-visible pattern honours the register without losing visibility.
  • Recompute readiness in the browser - Ship the raw tree to the client and compute readiness there.
    Not chosen because: Two implementations of the same compute are two chances to disagree. The server already walks the tree; piping the computed object into the HTML keeps the no-recompute invariant and makes the live-SSE path trivial.
  • Ship criterion-level diff in 0.29.0 - Render AC-level before-and-after inside the delta list, with a per-AC collapsible pane.
    Not chosen because: Open question 7 of the step 2 spec parks the AC-class before-and-after question for a UX review. Shipping without that review risks a design the review would reject; document-level diff carries the signal 0.29.0 needs.

ADR-4129... The intent-complete loop is harness-driven; rcf-lite computes questions with write-backs and never holds conversation state accepted

ADR-4129-questions-harness-driven-loop - The intent-complete loop is harness-driven; rcf-lite computes questions with write-backs and never holds conversation state

Status: accepted

Context: DEFINE step 3 (spec 2026-10-01, section 1.1) requires a product owner to reach `levels.intentComplete.ok === true` without an engineer. The question is whether rcf-lite should hold a conversation state (a stored loop file, a conversation engine) or stay stateless and let the harness (Claude Code or any MCP-wired agent) drive.

Decision: the loop is harness-driven; rcf-lite computes questions with write-backs and never holds conversation state. computeQuestions is a pure function of (readiness, tree, ledgers, profileText, persona); the harness runs the write-back a question carries, calls readiness again and asks the next question.

Consequences: The loop is monotone (each answer removes its item), the compute is testable in isolation, and the harness can be swapped without changing rcf-lite. The cost is that the harness must run readiness and questions each turn, which is a cheap pure call.

Alternatives considered

  • A conversation engine in rcf-lite - Hold an LLM-driven loop inside rcf-lite that elicits the PO directly.
    Not chosen because: An LLM dependency inside rcf-lite reverses the method's shape: rcf-lite is the referee the harness consults, not an agent of its own. It also forces a model and provider choice that the harness has already made.
  • A stored loop file - Keep a loop state file under rcf/define/ that tracks which question was asked last.
    Not chosen because: The stale state the detection model removed. A loop file would drift from the tree the moment any writer edits a ledger outside the loop, and would need its own validate pass; the four ledgers plus the profile already carry every state the loop needs.

ADR-4130... Intake is harness-split and tool-scanned; findings become open-question statements accepted

ADR-4130-intake-harness-split-tool-scanned - Intake is harness-split and tool-scanned; findings become open-question statements

Status: accepted

Context: DEFINE step 3 (spec 2026-10-01, section 2.1) requires a document intake path where a product owner hands over a folder and reaches `Intent-complete: yes` without an engineer driving. Splitting a source into kinded statements is the agent's job (the harness writes one statement file per source, operator corrects); the mechanical scans and the follow-up questions are rcf-lite's. The question is how finding-level signals (duplicates, contradictions, ambiguities) reach the loop.

Decision: intake is harness-split and tool-scanned; findings become open-question statements. The harness writes `<source>.statements.md` beside each source; `brief add --from` mints the statements and `runIntakeScansOnDelta` runs over the new ids against the existing body; every finding is appended as one `openQuestion` statement whose source names the scan and the ids involved. The loop then reads one check (`brief:openQuestions`) and the owner answers in one place.

Consequences: The owner sees findings as questions, not a separate list. One place carries intent (the brief ledger) and one check reads it. The harness can be swapped: any agent that writes the statement file shape and runs `brief add --from` reaches the same loop. The cost is that a finding's full detail lives inside the openQuestion text and its `scan:` source marker; a reviewer who wants a flat findings list builds it from `kind === 'openQuestion' && source startsWith 'scan:'`.

Alternatives considered

  • A separate findings list on the manifest - Keep an array of findings on rcf/manifest.json alongside the ledgers, read by the loop as a parallel surface.
    Not chosen because: A second place the loop would have to read, and a second place that could drift from the brief ledger. Making findings statements collapses two surfaces into the one the loop already needs.

ADR-4133... The Build/DAG canvas lays FBS by dependency depth, orders rows by buildOrder, measures the critical path by node count and parks unconnected FBS in a hidden lane with a count accepted

ADR-4133-dag-dependency-depth-layout - The Build/DAG canvas lays FBS by dependency depth, orders rows by buildOrder, measures the critical path by node count and parks unconnected FBS in a hidden lane with a count

Status: accepted

Context: The viewer UI refresh (design doc section 7) names a DAG for the Build tab's second sub-tab. The dogfood tree has 87 FBS: 46 declare no dependency, 36 are unconnected both ways, 1 is in progress and `estimatedHours` is sparse. A force-directed layout is unstable across reloads (the review surface is a diff-worthy artefact; identical trees must render identical pages), and grouping purely by `domain` hides the thing the DAG exists to show (which FBS feeds which). The v1 rcf-tools DAG proved the tiered layout works for the engineer audience the Build tab serves (decision 14); its gaps - dark-only palette, no inspector, orphan pile-up swamping the graph, no deep links, horizontal page scroll - are the ones this PR fixes.

Decision: Columns in the DAG are dependency-depth tiers computed from `dependsOnFbsIds` (0 for an FBS that declares no dependency; max over `depth(dep) + 1` otherwise). Rows inside a column are `buildOrder` ascending with `fbsId` lexicographic tie-break. Critical path is the longest chain by node count across the DAG, because `estimatedHours` is sparse on the dogfood tree (section 7 gap b); the critical-path chip highlights every member of that longest chain. Unconnected FBS - no incoming and no outgoing `dependsOnFbsIds` edge - sit in a lane below the main graph, hidden by default, with the count on the toggle. Cycle members (should any appear) are excluded from the depth layout and surfaced as a shared `findings-list` finding on the toolbar; non-cycle FBS still render so one bad edge never blocks the view (AC-204-6). The selection round-trips `#tab=build&sub=dag&entity=<id>` through the existing writeHash so a node is a link (decision 11, extended).

Consequences: The DAG is deterministic across reloads: same tree, same page. The depth tiers reflect what actually gates work, so the leftmost column is the "start here" set and buildable-now items concentrate on its right edge. Hiding unconnected FBS by default stops the 36-row pile-up swamping the dogfood tree - the toggle count makes them discoverable. Choosing node count for the critical path means the chip stays meaningful on the dogfood tree today and will only sharpen when `estimatedHours` fills in; the ADR explicitly leaves the hours-weighted critical path to a later change. Deep-link parity with Specs (`#tab=build&sub=specs&entity=<id>`) lets the inspector's Open-in-Specs link move cleanly across the two sub-tabs.

Alternatives considered

  • Force-directed layout - Lay nodes with a physics simulation and let the dependency edges settle.
    Not chosen because: Position jitters across reloads so screenshots and visual diffs are noisy; the review surface is diff-worthy by contract, and a layout that is not deterministic cannot be screenshotted into design evidence or compared across runs.
  • Group by domain only - Columns are areas (view, cli, build, ...) and rows are FBS in each area.
    Not chosen because: Hides the dependency structure that the DAG exists to show. Area is already a FilterBar facet on the Specs sub-tab and a badge on each node; adding a second encoding of it costs the dependency axis.
  • Hours-weighted critical path - Measure critical path by sum of `estimatedHours` along a chain.
    Not chosen because: `estimatedHours` is sparse on the dogfood tree (section 7 gap b); a weight that is missing on most nodes would silently bias the chip toward whichever subtree happens to have estimates. Node count is the honest signal today; the hours-weighted path becomes an opt-in once estimates are populated across the tree.
  • Render unconnected FBS inline (no lane) - Lay unconnected FBS as a 36-row column 0 alongside the connected tier 0.
    Not chosen because: Doubles the visual height of the leftmost column with nodes that have no edges, swamping the dependency graph the DAG exists to show. The toggled lane with the count keeps them one click away without the pile-up.
  • Block the DAG on any cycle - If the tree carries a `dependsOnFbsIds` cycle, refuse to render the DAG and show an error.
    Not chosen because: A bad edge on a 90-node graph should not take the view down; the `rcf validate` CLI is the enforcement surface. The DAG reports the cycle as a shared finding and renders the rest so the engineer can see what still composes.

1FBS-001 Document store core projectStructure AC3 medium complete

Build the document store: id-to-path resolution, JSON parse, schema validation against the registered bundle, persist-after-validate, and a tree walk from the manifest roots.

Approach

Register the published schema bundle once at start-up. Resolve ids to paths by the recommended layout convention. Make load and save the only filesystem touch points. Return structured errors rather than throwing strings, so every surface can report them consistently.

Acceptance criteria (3)

AC-101-1, AC-101-2, AC-101-3

Deliverables

  • Document store module with load, save and walkTree
  • Schema bundle registration at start-up
  • Structured error type for validation and reference failures
  • Init command that refuses to overwrite an existing project without an explicit force flag

Context

TACs: TAC-001

ADRs: ADR-001, ADR-002

TAD sections: systemOverview, integrationArchitecture

Show in the DAG

13FBS-013 Deploy-aware elicitation and hosting guidance guidance AC8 medium buildable notStarted

Harden the elicitation guidance so the deploy target is established early and constrains the stack, and so an owner who does not know their hosting is walked through choosing and configuring one in plain language. Edits the elicitation playbook and the harness fragment; no runtime subsystem.

Approach

In the elicitation playbook, add an early deploy-target elicitation item (asked before any stack is committed) and require the stack to be constrained by the answer and the decision captured as a project ADR. Add a hosting-choice walkthrough for the unsure owner: plain-language options, configuration steps (accounts, tokens, CLI), and honest isolation of the human-account-holder-only steps, modelled on the run-03 impersonation-refusal framing. Add a harness-fragment rule that a stack must not be committed before the deploy target is established. Extend the guidance drift tests to assert the new content invariants. All changes are to shipped guidance/prompt surface; the deploy target is elicited by the agent, not by rcf init (init is bootstrap-only since the v0.2.1 UX pass).

Acceptance criteria (8)

AC-802-1, AC-802-2, AC-802-3, AC-802-4, AC-803-1, AC-803-2, AC-803-3, AC-803-4

  • Elicitation playbook: early deploy-target item and stack-constraint rule
  • Elicitation playbook: jargon-free hosting-choice walkthrough with honest account-holder-step isolation
  • Harness fragment rule: no stack before the deploy target is established
  • Guidance drift tests for the new content invariants

14FBS-014 Local-preview default, runtime-honest verification, interim self-review guidance AC12 large buildable notStarted

Harden the build-cycle guidance so every build lands a documented local preview as its default outcome, every verification claim names the runtime it was checked against, and the method carries interim fresh-context self-review guidance. Edits the build-cycle playbook, the build-cycle contract and the harness fragment; no runtime subsystem.

Approach

In the build-cycle guidance, make a working, documented local preview loop (dev server, seeded data where needed, ideally one command) a required, hosting-independent part of a build's definition of done. Require every 'verified'/'tested' claim - in the Test and Finalise stages and in the PR body's verification section - to name the runtime it was checked against, forbid any claim implying deploy-runtime verification that did not happen, and add an explicit labelled-claim example. Add an interim self-review section describing a periodic and end-of-build fresh-context reviewer dispatch that drives the app against its ACs, targeting session-class bugs, false-promise UI, runtime mismatch, dead auth paths and dead code, scoped honestly as a stopgap until rcf verify-lite and explicitly not the independent gate. Add matching harness-fragment rules and extend the guidance drift tests.

Acceptance criteria (12)

AC-801-1, AC-801-2, AC-801-3, AC-801-4, AC-804-1, AC-804-2, AC-804-3, AC-804-4, AC-805-1, AC-805-2, AC-805-3, AC-805-4

Deliverables

  • Build-cycle guidance: local preview loop as default, hosting-independent definition-of-done item
  • Build-cycle and PR-authoring guidance: runtime-provenance labelling with a worked example
  • Build-cycle guidance: interim self-review section, honestly scoped away from the independent gate
  • Harness fragment rules and guidance drift tests for the new invariants

15FBS-015 `rcf verify` group routing (0.10.0 CLI reorganisation) cli AC3 small complete

Route the adversarial ship-gate verifier under the unified `rcf` CLI as `rcf verify <run|report|provision|cleanup|mcp|browser>`. The legacy standalone `rcf-verify` bin (0.7.1 transition-grace alias) is deleted outright; consumers move to `rcf verify <verb>` in one hop.

Approach

bin/rcf.js declares a `verify` entry in the top-level GROUPS map whose sub-verbs (run, report, provision, cleanup, mcp, browser) resolve to the corresponding main() exports from src/verify/cli/*.js and src/cli/browser-verify.js. The unified CLI's help output lists the verify group with its sub-verbs, sourced from the per-verb HELP exports via HELP_MAP.verify (single-source rule). The dispatcher additionally recognises pre-0.10.0 flat verb tokens through OLD_FLAT_MAP: on match it writes a one-line stderr hint naming the new grouped form before exiting 2. This is a usage-error affordance, not a fallback; the invocation fails.

Acceptance criteria (3)

AC-901-1, AC-901-2, AC-901-3

Deliverables

  • bin/rcf.js: `verify` on the top-level GROUPS map, dispatching per sub-verb to the verify-suite handlers plus browser-verify
  • bin/rcf.js: OLD_FLAT_MAP recognises pre-0.10.0 flat verbs and emits a stderr hint at the new grouped form before exit 2
  • package.json: `bin` field carries only `rcf`; the historical `rcf-verify` entry and bin/rcf-verify.js file are deleted
  • src/cli/help.js: verify group header + sub-verb catalogue in TOP_LEVEL_HELP; `rcf help verify` prints the group help; `rcf help verify <verb>` prints per-verb help via HELP_MAP

16FBS-016 Blueprint verb family (add, list, remove, upgrade) with manifest.blueprints[] writes cli AC5 medium buildable notStarted

Introduce the `rcf define blueprint <verb>` verb family and its manifest-writing path. Adds `src/blueprint/` module (loader, applier, contribution-writer) and `src/cli/blueprint.js` (parseArgs, dispatch, HELP block). Adds `blueprint` to the top-level SUBCOMMANDS map on `bin/rcf.js` and to the `TOP_LEVEL` block on `src/cli/help.js` so `rcf --help` advertises it. Every apply writes an entry to `manifest.blueprints[]` per the 0.4.4 schema (slug, version, appliedAt, source, namespace, contributions[]). `add` is idempotent on a clean re-apply; `remove` refuses when any project-authored doc references a contribution id.

Approach

One dispatcher, one loader, one applier, one writer. bin/rcf.js gains `blueprint: blueprintMain` on SUBCOMMANDS; src/cli/blueprint.js parses `add|list|remove|upgrade` and dispatches to src/blueprint/ handlers. Blueprint loading is a small package-metadata reader (slug, version, ADR contributions with optional scope, doc contributions manifest); Phase 1 keeps the resolver `file://` and `link:` only, with the registry/git-ref shape captured in the source string so the schema forward-compat holds. Contribution writing goes through the existing store writer paths so a blueprint apply produces the same doc files a hand-created doc would. Removal is a manifest patch + contribution-path unlink; the referring-doc check reuses the existing tree walker to enumerate every string field for id occurrences.

Acceptance criteria (5)

AC-1001-1, AC-1001-2, AC-1001-3, AC-1001-4, AC-1001-5

Deliverables

  • src/cli/blueprint.js: parseArgs + HELP + main() dispatching add/list/remove/upgrade
  • src/blueprint/index.js: barrel re-exporting apply, list, remove, upgrade, loadBlueprint, detectGlobalAdrConflicts
  • src/blueprint/apply.js: apply(tree, blueprint, opts) — idempotency + conflict detection + contribution writes + manifest update
  • src/blueprint/loader.js: loadBlueprint(source) — reads a blueprint's metadata (slug, version, ADR contributions with scope, doc contributions)
  • src/blueprint/remove.js: remove(tree, slug, opts) — referring-doc scan + manifest patch + file unlinks
  • src/blueprint/list.js: list(tree) — reads manifest.blueprints[] and returns rows
  • bin/rcf.js: `blueprint: blueprintMain` on SUBCOMMANDS
  • src/cli/help.js: `blueprint <verb>` on the TOP_LEVEL block, `help blueprint` prints the blueprint HELP
  • test/blueprint/apply.test.js, list.test.js, remove.test.js, cli.test.js — behaviour tests keyed to AC-1001-1..5
